documents.t: Audit Logs give you a detailed, searchable record of authentication events on your site. Every login attempt, registration, password reset, OAuth flow, 2FA challenge, API key action, and settings change can be captured and stored in your WordPress database. Audit logging is disabled by default. Enable it in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Audit Logs → Config.
Toggle the Enable Audit Logging switch at the top of the Audit Logs configuration page.

Choose which events to capture. You can enable all events at once using the Enable All button, or pick individual events using the checkboxes. Use the search box to filter the list. The full list of trackable events: Authentication events​ Event key Label Description auth.login.success Login Success A JWT was successfully generated for a user auth.login.failed Login Failed Authentication failed (wrong credentials, disabled, etc.) auth.logout.success Logout (Token Revoked) A JWT was successfully revoked auth.logout.failed Logout Failed Token revocation failed auth.register.success Register Success A new WordPress user was created via the API auth.register.failed Register Failed User registration failed auth.password_reset.request Password Reset Request A password reset code was requested auth.password_reset.success Password Reset Success Password successfully changed auth.password_reset.failed Password Reset Failed Password change failed auth.delete_user.success Delete User Success A user account was deleted via the API auth.delete_user.failed Delete User Failed User deletion failed auth.login_session.success Auto-Login Session Success Auto-login via JWT completed successfully auth.login_session.failed Auto-Login Session Failed Auto-login via JWT failed auth.refresh_token.success Refresh Token Success A JWT was successfully refreshed auth.refresh_token.failed Refresh Token Failed Token refresh failed auth.oauth.success OAuth Login Success OAuth authentication completed successfully auth.oauth.failed OAuth Login Failed OAuth authentication failed Two-Factor Authentication events​ Event key Label Description auth.2fa.challenge_issued 2FA Challenge Issued A 2FA challenge was sent to the user auth.2fa.verify_success 2FA Verification Success 2FA code verified successfully auth.2fa.verify_failed 2FA Verification Failed 2FA code verification failed Settings events​ Event key Label Description settings.save.success Settings Saved Plugin settings were saved by an admin note Since version 4.1.0, the Settings Saved entry never stores secrets in plain text: auth codes, JWT decryption rule keys and webhook header values are shown as [REDACTED]. API Key events​ Event key Label Description api_key.create.success API Key Created A new API key was created api_key.create.failed API Key Create Failed API key creation failed api_key.update.success API Key Updated An API key was updated api_key.update.failed API Key Update Failed API key update failed api_key.revoke.success API Key Revoked An API key was revoked api_key.revoke.failed API Key Revoke Failed API key revocation failed api_key.delete.success API Key Deleted An API key was deleted api_key.delete.failed API Key Delete Failed API key deletion failed api_key.used API Key Used A request was authenticated using an API key AI Ability events​ Event key Label Description ai.ability.success AI Ability Executed An AI agent ran a Simple JWT Login ability successfully ai.ability.failed AI Ability Failed An AI agent ran an ability and it failed WP-CLI events​ Available since version 4.3.0. Only commands that change data are recorded. The user is the one passed with the global WP-CLI --user=<user> flag. Event key Label Description cli.command.success WP-CLI Command Executed A wp jwt command completed cli.command.failed WP-CLI Command Failed A wp jwt command failed

Set how many days to keep log entries. Entries older than this threshold are automatically purged by a scheduled WordPress cron job. The minimum value is 1 day. Default: 90 days. tip For compliance use cases (GDPR, SOC 2, etc.), set the retention period to match your data-retention policy. For high-traffic sites, a shorter window keeps the database table from growing too large.

Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → Audit Logs → Logs to view the stored entries. Each entry records: Event - the event key (for example, auth.login.success) User ID - the WordPress user involved (where applicable) User Email - the email of the user involved Status - success or failed Details - additional context (for example, changed setting keys) IP Address - the client IP that triggered the event Timestamp - when the event occurred

Audit log writes are dispatched after the API response is sent to the client - they never block or delay the response your app receives. The plugin uses PHP's fastcgi_finish_request() to flush the response first, then write the log entry in the same PHP process. If that function is unavailable (see table below), the log write happens synchronously before the response is returned. Database writes are fast, so this rarely causes noticeable latency. Server environment Async logging nginx + PHP-FPM (standard nginx setup) Yes - response flushed before log is written Apache + PHP-FPM (mod_proxy_fcgi) Yes - response flushed before log is written Apache + mod_php No - log write blocks the response LiteSpeed / OpenLiteSpeed Depends on version - generally no

Security monitoring - track failed login attempts and unusual activity patterns Compliance - demonstrate an audit trail for authentication events Debugging - reproduce exact event sequences when troubleshooting user-reported issues Change tracking - see exactly which settings were modified and when via settings.save.success

Every authentication and 2FA event above also fires a WordPress action, such as simple_jwt_login_audit_auth_login_failed, so your own code can react to it. The action fires only when audit logging is enabled and the event is selected. See Audit Hooks for the full list and arguments.
Send events to other services with webhooks React to audit events in PHP with audit hooks

Auth Codes are an optional security layer that adds a shared secret to your API requests. Think of them as API keys: a caller must include the correct code alongside their request, otherwise the plugin rejects it. You can require an Auth Code for any combination of the following operations: Auto-login Register User Delete User Reset Password and Change Password Authenticate (JWT generation) caution Use long, random strings for Auth Code values. Short or predictable codes offer little protection. Treat them like passwords - store them securely and rotate them if they are compromised.
Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → Auth Codes to configure.

The query parameter name (or body field name) clients must use to pass the code in requests. Default: AUTH_KEY. ?AUTH_KEY=THISISMySpeCiaLAUthCode Change this if you want to avoid exposing that your site uses Simple JWT Login, or if you need to avoid a name collision.
Each code is a row with three fields - add as many codes as you need. You can have different codes for different purposes (for example, one for mobile apps, one for server-to-server integrations).

Each Auth Code has three fields: Field Description Authentication Key The actual code value that must be included in requests using the Auth Code URL Key parameter name (default: AUTH_KEY). WordPress User Role (Optional) When set, users registered using this code are assigned this role instead of the default role configured in Register Settings. Useful for creating multiple user tiers (for example, "premium" vs "free") from a single endpoint. Expiration Date (Optional) The date and time after which this code is no longer accepted. Format: Y-M-D H:m:s - for example, 2025-12-31 23:59:59. note Leaving the expiration date blank means the code never expires.

WordPress REST API JWT authentication starts here: send WordPress credentials to this endpoint and get back a signed JWT. The returned token can then be included in subsequent requests to protected endpoints or used to auto-login users. You can authenticate using any of the following combinations: email + password - standard credential pair username + password - use the WordPress username instead of email login + password - mirrors the WordPress login page behavior; accepts either email or username API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth Keep credentials out of the URL Send the email and password in the request body (JSON, as shown below), never in the query string. URLs are written to server logs, proxy logs, browser history, and monitoring tools. PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description email required* string User email address. Required when username and login are absent. username required* string WordPress username. Required when email and login are absent. login required* string WordPress username or email. Simulates the WordPress login page flow. Required when email and username are absent. password required* string User plain-text password. Required when password_hash is absent. password_hash optional string The user's hashed password as stored in the database. Required when password is absent. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key configured in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). payload optional string | object Extra claims merged into the JWT payload. Send a JSON-encoded string for form-encoded requests, or a native JSON object for JSON body requests. Reserved claims are always overridden by the authenticated user's data and cannot be set this way.

{ "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "password": "SomeSuperSecretPassword" } With username and password hash: { "username": "myuser", "password_hash": "PasswordStoredInTheDB" } With login (accepts email or username) and auth code: { "login": "username or email", "password": "SomeSuperSecretPassword", "AUTH_KEY": "MySecretAuthCode" } With extra payload claims (JSON body - native object): { "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "password": "SomeSuperSecretPassword", "payload": { "department": "engineering", "region": "eu" } } With extra payload claims (form-encoded body - JSON-encoded string): email=test@simplejwtlogin.com&password=SomeSuperSecretPassword&payload={"department":"engineering","region":"eu"}

{ "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c", "refresh_token": "a1b2c3d4e5f678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012" } } refresh_token is only present when the refresh token feature is enabled in plugin settings.
Bad request - required parameters are missing. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Email or username is required.", "error_code": 46 } }
Unauthorized - credentials are incorrect or the auth code is invalid. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Wrong user credentials.", "error_code": 48 } }
Forbidden - authentication is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Authentication is not enabled.", "error_code": 45 } }
Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 16 } }
curl -X POST https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"test@simplejwtlogin.com","password":"mySecretPassword"}'

$simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->authenticate('email@simplejwtlogin.com', 'your password', 'AUTH CODE');

All error responses follow the standard envelope: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Human-readable error description", "error_code": 48 } } Common error codes: Code Meaning 45 Authentication is not enabled in plugin settings. 46 Email or username is missing from the request. 47 Password is missing from the request. 48 Credentials are incorrect.

Since version 4.2.0, the password is checked with WordPress's wp_authenticate(), the same way as wp-login.php: Brute-force and user-block plugins (Limit Login Attempts, Wordfence and similar) protect /auth too. Every failed attempt - unknown user, wrong password or wrong hash - fires the wp_login_failed action, so those plugins count it. Application passwords can't be exchanged for a JWT. Unknown logins take the same password hashing time as known ones, so response timing doesn't reveal which accounts exist. warning Authenticating with password_hash lets anyone holding a database dump get JWTs without cracking the hashes, and login protection plugins don't apply to it. Keep it disabled unless you really need it - the AI Abilities security report flags it.
Configure the authentication feature under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Authentication.
Enable or disable the authentication endpoint. When disabled, POST /auth returns a 403 error.
When enabled, every authentication request must include a valid Auth Code. The parameter name is the Auth Code URL Key from the Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).

Base64-encoded password​ Enable when the password or password_hash value is Base64-encoded before sending. Useful when passwords contain special characters (including ', " and \) that would be mangled in query string parameters. Since version 4.2.0, a value that isn't valid Base64 gets the "Wrong user credentials." error.

The JWT header always includes the standard alg and typ fields. You can add extra static key-value pairs to the header using Custom Header Claims. The following header fields are reserved and cannot be overwritten by custom claims: typ, alg, kid. Example JWT header with a custom claim: { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT", "x-app-id": "my-app" }

Choose which user data fields are included in the JWT payload. At minimum, iat (issued-at timestamp) is always present. Claim Description iat Unix timestamp when the JWT was issued. Always included, cannot be removed. exp Unix timestamp when the JWT expires. If omitted, the token never expires. email The authenticated user's email address. id The WordPress user ID. site The site URL where the token was generated. username The WordPress user_login value. iss Issuer claim. The value is taken from the Issuer value field below. Issuer (iss)​ When iss is enabled in the payload, this field sets its value. Defaults to the site URL if left blank. Used to identify the token's origin, especially in multi-provider setups. Custom Payload Claims​ Add static key-value pairs to the JWT payload. These are injected into every token generated by the plugin. To add claims on a per-request basis instead, use the payload parameter on POST /auth. The following payload keys are reserved and cannot be overwritten - either from these settings or from the payload request parameter: iat, exp, email, id, site, username, iss. Example: { "iat": 1718000000, "exp": 1718003600, "email": "user@example.com", "id": 42, "department": "engineering", "app_version": "2.1.0" }

How long (in minutes) the generated JWT is valid. After this period the token is rejected by the plugin's validation and auto-login endpoints. Default: 60 minutes. Set to 0 to disable expiry (not recommended for production).

Expected audience​ Available since version 4.2.0. Optional. When set, new JWTs from /auth, /auth/refresh, register and OAuth carry this value in the aud claim, and a JWT signed with the plugin key is only accepted when its aud (a string or a list) contains it. This stops another site or app that shares the same signing key or issuer from using its JWTs on your site. A good value is your site URL. JWTs issued before you set it have no aud and are rejected with error code 130 - users must log in again (a refresh token still gets a new JWT). For JWTs matched by a JWT Rule, set the Expected audience (aud) on the rule instead.

Available since version 4.2.0, off by default. When on, changing a user's password deletes that user's refresh tokens and rejects every JWT issued before the change, so a stolen token stops working once the password is reset. It applies to: the plugin's reset password endpoint the wp-login.php lost password form on WordPress 5.8+, profile and admin edits and /wp/v2/users updates since version 4.2.0, any password set with wp_set_password() - for example, the Two Factor compromised-password reset, WP-CLI or other plugins Rejected JWTs return error code 55. JWTs without an iat claim (for example, issued by an external service through JWT Rules) are then also rejected for that user.

Restrict authentication requests to a comma-separated list of trusted IP addresses. Leave blank to allow requests from any IP. 192.0.1.1, 192.2.2.2 The wildcard * is supported in any octet, which is useful for allowing an entire subnet: 85.*.*.*, 86.*.*.*
Refresh the JWT or revoke it on logout Use the JWT in a Next.js app or a Flutter app Troubleshoot JWT errors

The Autologin endpoint lets you log a user into WordPress by passing a valid JWT - no username or password form needed. This is ideal for: Magic-link emails - generate a signed link and email it to the user SSO flows - redirect users from an external system directly into WordPress Mobile apps - open a webview session without re-prompting for credentials Cross-domain redirects - seamlessly land users on a specific page after authentication The plugin validates the JWT, identifies the WordPress user from the token payload, creates the authenticated session, and redirects the user to the configured destination. API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: GET ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin&JWT={{JWT}}&AUTH_KEY={{AUTH_KEY_VALUE}} Parameter Type Description JWT required string Your JWT. Can alternatively be passed as Authorization: Bearer <token>. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). redirectUrl optional string If provided and "Honor the redirectUrl parameter" is enabled in settings, the user is redirected here after a successful login instead of the configured destination. Parameters can be sent as query params.

https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin&JWT={{JWT}}&AUTH_KEY={{AUTH_KEY_VALUE}} Or via Authorization header: GET /wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_HERE
The browser is redirected (HTTP 302) to the WordPress site or the custom redirectUrl. The response body is empty HTML; the redirect is handled via HTTP headers.
Bad request - unclassified error (for example, malformed JWT encoding). { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Invalid JWT.", "error_code": 25 } }
Unauthorized - JWT is invalid, has a bad signature, is expired, is revoked, or the auth code is wrong. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "JWT has expired.", "error_code": 14 } }
Forbidden - auto-login is disabled in plugin settings, or the client IP is not on the allow-list. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Auto-login is not enabled.", "error_code": 26 } }
The WordPress user identified by the JWT payload could not be found. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "User not found.", "error_code": 24 } }
Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }
curl 'https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin&JWT=mysecretjwt&AUTH_KEY=mysecretauthcode'

Using the simple-jwt-login PHP Client: $simpleJWT = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $url = $simpleJWT->login('Your JWT'); header('Location: ' . $url);
var JWT = 'myJWT'; var AUTH_KEY = 'MY_SECRET_AUTH_CODE'; window.location.href = 'https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/autologin&JWT=' + JWT + '&AUTH_KEY=' + AUTH_KEY;

All error responses follow the standard envelope: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Human-readable error description", "error_code": 26 } } Common error codes: Code Meaning 23 JWT is missing from the auto-login request. 24 User not found - no WordPress user matches the JWT claims. 26 Auto-login is not enabled in plugin settings. 27 Invalid Auth Code provided. 28 Client IP is not on the allowed IP list. 29 The configured JWT payload property (sub-key) could not be found in the token. 30 The configured JWT payload property (user key) could not be found in the token. 68 The JWT issuer (iss) is not on the allowed list. JWT decoding errors (1-22) may also appear when the supplied token cannot be parsed or its signature is invalid.
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Autologin.

Enable or disable the autologin endpoint. When disabled, all GET requests to /autologin return a 403 error. When enabled, users can log in by passing a valid JWT via URL parameter or Authorization: Bearer header.

When enabled, an additional Auth Code must be provided alongside the JWT to allow login. The parameter name is the Auth Code URL Key from Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). Configure the codes themselves in the Auth Codes tab.

Controls where users are sent after login succeeds or fails. After successful login, redirect to: Option Description Dashboard Redirects to the WordPress admin panel (/wp-admin/). Homepage Redirects to the site's front page. No redirect No HTTP redirect is performed; the response is returned directly. Custom URL Redirects to the URL you specify in the text field below the options. On login failure, redirect to: Enter a URL to redirect the user when login fails (for example, expired token, invalid auth code). Leave blank to return an error JSON response without redirecting. On the failure redirect page you can display the error message returned by the plugin using the simple-jwt-login:request shortcode: [simple-jwt-login:request key="error_message"]

Pass login request parameters to the redirect URL​ When enabled, the login request parameters are appended to the redirect URL as query string arguments. Since version 4.2.0, the JWT itself is never copied, whatever its URL key is (see JWT Input Sources in General settings) and in any letter case (for example, ?Jwt=). Strip these parameters from the redirect URL​ Comma-separated list of query parameters to remove after redirect (for example, auth_code). Matching ignores letter case. Useful for cleaning sensitive values out of the browser address bar. Leave blank to keep all parameters. Honor the redirectUrl query parameter as a redirect override​ When enabled, including redirectUrl in the autologin request overrides the configured redirect destination. This allows per-request redirect targets, useful for magic-link emails that need to land users on a specific page. Available URL template variables: Use these placeholders in your custom redirect URL or in the redirectUrl parameter. They are replaced with actual values at redirect time. Variable Description {{site_url}} The site URL {{user_id}} The logged-in user's ID {{user_email}} The logged-in user's email address {{user_login}} The logged-in user's username {{user_first_name}} The user's first name {{user_last_name}} The user's last name {{user_nicename}} The user's URL-friendly name Example: https://yourdomain.com/profile?uid={{user_id}}&site={{site_url}}

Restrict autologin to requests from specific sources. Leave fields blank to allow all. Allowed IP Addresses​ Comma-separated list of IP addresses allowed to use the autologin endpoint. Leave blank to allow all IPs. Allowed JWT Issuers (iss)​ Comma-separated list of accepted iss (issuer) claim values. When set, a JWT whose iss does not match any value in this list is rejected with error code 68. Leave blank to accept any issuer.

In the plugin settings, set the "JWT Parameter Key" field to the name of the JWT payload property that holds the user identifier. For example, if your JWT payload looks like this: { "sub": "1234567890", "name": "John Doe", "UserID": 123456 } Set JWT Parameter Key to UserID. The plugin uses that value to look up the WordPress user.

Simple JWT Login registers a wp jwt command namespace in WP-CLI. It covers the plugin's main operations: initial setup, issuing and revoking JWTs, signing key rotation, API keys, auth codes, settings, diagnostics, audit logs, and webhooks. The commands run in the WordPress process on the server, so they do not need HTTP access to the site. wp jwt --help wp jwt config --help Since version 4.3.0 The commands are part of the plugin. The separate Simple JWT Login CLI add-on is deprecated and no longer needed. While the add-on is active, the built-in commands are not registered, General > CLI defaults to off, and the CLI card in the admin shows a warning. Deactivate and delete the add-on to switch to the built-in commands. Scripts written for the add-on may need changes - see Migrating from the add-on. On versions before 4.3.0, the commands are only available through the add-on.

The commands are enabled by default. To disable them, turn off Simple JWT Login > General > CLI, or run: wp jwt config set cli.enabled 0 Once disabled, wp jwt is no longer registered, so it can only be turned back on from the admin. warning Anyone who can run WP-CLI on the server can issue a JWT for any user, administrators included (wp jwt generate), and read the signing key (wp jwt config get). Restrict shell access, or disable the commands on servers where WP-CLI access is shared.

Command Description wp jwt setup Generate a signing key if there is none and enable /auth wp jwt login Authenticate a user with a password and print a JWT wp jwt generate Issue a JWT for a user without a password wp jwt refresh Exchange a refresh token for a new JWT wp jwt decode Print the claims of a JWT (signature not verified) wp jwt validate Verify signature, expiry, audience, user, and revocation wp jwt revoke Revoke a JWT and delete the user's refresh tokens wp jwt revoke-all Revoke every JWT and refresh token of a user wp jwt key generate / rotate Print a new signing key, or replace the stored one wp jwt api-key create / list / revoke Manage API keys wp jwt auth-code list / add / remove Manage auth codes wp jwt config get / set / list / export / import Read and change the settings wp jwt doctor Versions, REST URLs, endpoint status, and configuration warnings wp jwt security-report Security score (0-100, grade A-F) and findings wp jwt explain-error Meaning, HTTP status and related settings of an error code wp jwt log list / analyze Query and summarize the audit log wp jwt webhook list / test / logs List webhooks, send a test call, read the call log wp jwt cleanup Run the daily cleanup job immediately

Commands that return a single result accept --format=text (default) or --format=json. Commands that return a list accept --format=table (default), csv, json, yaml or count, and --fields=a,b to select columns. A <user> argument accepts a user ID, login, or email, the same as wp user get. Commands that change data ask for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt in scripts. Global WP-CLI flags work as usual, for example --url=<site> on Multisite or --path=<dir>. note With the audit log enabled, commands that change data are recorded as cli.command.success or cli.command.failed (enable the events in Audit Logs). The entry uses the WordPress user passed with the global --user=<user> flag. A command that disables the audit log is still recorded.

The REST API is built for client applications. The CLI is built for the people who operate the site: developers, DevOps, support, and security. The examples below show where wp jwt replaces manual work in the admin or custom scripts.

A fresh WordPress install needs a signing key and an enabled /auth endpoint before a frontend can log in. wp jwt setup does both, so a docker compose up or a provisioning script produces a working environment without opening the admin. wp plugin install simple-jwt-login --activate wp jwt setup --algorithm=HS256 wp jwt config import ./config/jwt.json --merge --yes # project defaults, see "Configuration as code"

Integration and end-to-end tests need a valid JWT. With wp jwt generate, the pipeline gets a short-lived token for a dedicated test user, so no WordPress password has to be stored in CI secrets. TOKEN=$(wp jwt generate ci-bot --ttl=10) # valid for 10 minutes curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ https://staging.example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me wp jwt revoke "$TOKEN" # invalidate it when the job ends

documents.t: Keep the plugin settings in the repository and apply them on deploy. Changes go through code review, and --dry-run prints the exact diff (secret values masked) before anything is saved. # Once, on the reference environment wp jwt config export --file=config/jwt.json # In the deploy pipeline wp jwt config import config/jwt.json --merge --dry-run wp jwt config import config/jwt.json --merge --yes warning The export contains the signing key and other secrets. Remove them from the file before committing it, and set them per environment with wp jwt config set or in wp-config.php. Import such a file with --merge: a full import replaces the whole settings object and would drop the stored keys.

Fail a pipeline when the configuration has critical findings, for example a short signing key or a public endpoint without an auth code. wp jwt security-report --min-severity=critical --format=json \ | jq -e '.findings | length == 0' > /dev/null \ || { wp jwt security-report --min-severity=critical; exit 1; }

wp jwt key rotate replaces the signing key without invalidating issued tokens: tokens signed before the rotation are accepted until they expire. This makes periodic rotation safe to run from cron. # crontab: rotate the signing key on the 1st of every month 0 3 1 * * cd /var/www/html && wp jwt key rotate --yes

When a token, a device or a signing key is compromised, the response is a few commands instead of a database edit. wp jwt revoke-all jane@example.com --yes # one user: every JWT and refresh token wp jwt key rotate --immediate --yes # leaked key: every issued token stops working wp jwt log analyze --hours=24 # failure rates, top failing IPs and users wp jwt log list --status=failure --per-page=100 --format=csv > incident.csv

Create a scoped, expiring API key for a partner or a service, and revoke it when the contract ends. The key value is printed once, at creation. wp jwt api-key create integrations --name="Partner ACME" \ --permissions=read --expires-at="2027-06-30 23:59:59" --format=json wp jwt api-key list --fields=id,name,key_prefix,expires_at,last_used_at wp jwt api-key revoke 7

Check a webhook URL and its headers before enabling it in production. test sends a test payload even when the webhook is disabled and fails on a non-2xx response. wp jwt webhook list wp jwt webhook test 0 --event=login

When a client reports an error, the support engineer can check the token and the configuration on the server directly. wp jwt explain-error 48 # what errorCode 48 means and which settings to check wp jwt decode "$TOKEN" --format=json # claims, without verifying the signature wp jwt validate "$TOKEN" # the same checks the endpoints run wp jwt doctor # endpoints, REST URLs and configuration warnings

Prepares a site to issue JWTs: generates a signing key when the configured algorithm has none, enables Authentication, and prints the /auth URL with a sample curl request. wp jwt setup [--algorithm=<algorithm>] [--force] Option Required Description --algorithm=<algorithm> No HS256, HS384, HS512, RS256, RS384, RS512, or random. Default: the configured algorithm. A different algorithm always gets a new key --force No Generate a new key even if one exists A replaced key keeps validating the tokens it signed until they expire, the same as wp jwt key rotate. Keys defined in wp-config.php are not changed, and in that case the algorithm can not be changed from the command line. wp jwt setup # keep the existing key, enable /auth wp jwt setup --algorithm=RS256 # switch to RS256 with a new RSA key pair wp jwt setup --force # new key, same algorithm

Authenticates a WordPress user with a password and prints a JWT. note Authentication > Allow Authentication must be enabled, or run wp jwt config set authorization.enabled 1. wp jwt login [--username=<username>] [--email=<email>] [--login=<login>] [--password=<password>] [--format=<format>] Option Required Description --username=<username> One identifier WordPress username --email=<email> One identifier WordPress user email --login=<login> One identifier Username or email - tried as username first, then as email --password=<password> No The user's password. If omitted, it is read from a hidden prompt or from STDIN, so it does not end up in the shell history --format=<format> No text (default) or json When more than one identifier is passed, the priority is --username > --email > --login. When Refresh Token is enabled, a refresh token is stored the same as on /auth. Users with two-factor authentication can not get a JWT from the command line. wp jwt login --username=admin # prompts for the password wp jwt login --email=admin@example.com --format=json < password.txt # {"jwt":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."} TOKEN=$(wp jwt login --username=admin < password.txt) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me

Issues a JWT for a user without their password. The token has the same claims and signing key as one from /auth. Two-factor authentication is not applied. When Refresh Token is enabled, a refresh token is printed too. wp jwt generate <user> [--ttl=<minutes>] [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <user> Yes User ID, login, or email --ttl=<minutes> No Expiration in minutes, minimum 1. Defaults to Authentication > JWT TTL --format=<format> No text (default) or json. In text format without a refresh token, only the JWT is printed, so the output can be assigned to a variable TOKEN=$(wp jwt generate admin --ttl=10) wp jwt generate 42 --format=json # {"jwt":"eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...","refresh_token":"3f2a..."}

Exchanges a refresh token for a new JWT and a new refresh token, like /auth/refresh. The endpoint checks apply. Refresh Token must be enabled, Allowed IPs must be empty (a CLI request has no client IP), and the auth code is required when the endpoint requires one. The old refresh token is invalidated. wp jwt refresh <refresh-token> [--auth-code=<code>] [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <refresh-token> Yes A refresh token from /auth, wp jwt login or wp jwt generate --auth-code=<code> If the refresh endpoint requires an auth code The auth code --format=<format> No text (default) or json wp jwt refresh 3f2a...c9 # jwt eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi... # refresh_token 8b1d...e4 wp jwt refresh 3f2a...c9 --auth-code=MY_CODE --format=json | jq -r '.jwt'

Prints the payload of a JWT. The signature is not verified - use wp jwt validate for that. wp jwt decode <token> [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <token> Yes The JWT --format=<format> No text (default, one claim value line per claim) or json wp jwt decode eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpZCI6MSwiZXhwIjoxOTk5OTk5fQ.sig # id 1 # exp 1999999 wp jwt decode "$TOKEN" --format=json | jq '.exp'

Validates a JWT with the same checks as the plugin endpoints: JWT rules, signature, expiry, audience, user, and revocation. wp jwt validate <token> [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <token> Yes The JWT --format=<format> No text (default) or json ({"valid":true,"message":"..."}) The exit code is 1 when the token is not valid, so the command can be used directly in if statements and CI steps. wp jwt validate "$TOKEN" # valid yes # message Token is valid. if wp jwt validate "$TOKEN" > /dev/null; then echo "Token OK" fi tip validate and revoke need the signing key and algorithm (General), and the Login > Login by setting must match a claim in the token.

Revokes a JWT. The signature is verified first, and the user's refresh tokens are deleted, the same as the revoke endpoint. wp jwt revoke <token> [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <token> Yes The JWT to revoke --format=<format> No text (default) or json wp jwt revoke "$TOKEN" # success yes # message Token has been revoked.

Revokes every JWT and refresh token issued to a user up to now, for example after a leaked token or a lost device. It works whether or not Revoke tokens on password change is enabled. Tokens issued afterwards (from the next second) are valid. wp jwt revoke-all <user> [--yes] Option Required Description <user> Yes User ID, login, or email --yes No Skip the confirmation prompt wp jwt revoke-all jane@example.com # prompts: "Revoke every token of jane?" wp jwt revoke-all 42 --yes

wp jwt key generate [--algorithm=<algorithm>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt key rotate [--algorithm=<algorithm>] [--immediate] [--show] [--yes] Option Command Description --algorithm=<algorithm> both HS256, HS384, HS512, RS256, RS384, RS512, or random (the selected algorithm is printed). Default: the configured algorithm --format=<format> generate text (default: the key, or the private then the public PEM) or json (algorithm and the key fields) --immediate rotate Do not keep the old key: every token signed with it, or with a key kept by an earlier rotation, is rejected immediately --show rotate Print the new key. Without it, the key is only saved --yes rotate Skip the confirmation prompt generate prints a key without saving it: random bytes the size of the hash, hex encoded, for HS256/384/512, or an RSA key pair for RS256 (2048 bits), RS384 (3072 bits) and RS512 (4096 bits). rotate saves a new key (and a new algorithm, with --algorithm) without breaking issued tokens: New tokens are signed with the new key. The old key is moved to a JWT Rule that matches tokens with iat less than the rotation time, so tokens issued before the rotation stay valid until they expire. The daily cleanup (or wp jwt cleanup, or the next rotation) removes that rule once the JWT TTL plus 60 seconds has passed. Refresh tokens keep working: when no Refresh Token key is set, the old key becomes the refresh token key. Your own JWT rules are not changed and are evaluated before the rotation rules. A key defined in wp-config.php must be changed there. warning Until its rule is removed, the old key still validates tokens. If a key leaked, use --immediate. Tokens that live longer than the JWT TTL (wp jwt generate --ttl, or a payload without exp) stop working when the rule is removed. wp jwt key generate --algorithm=HS512 # print a key to use elsewhere wp jwt key generate --algorithm=RS256 --format=json # RSA key pair as JSON wp jwt key rotate --yes # scheduled rotation, issued tokens stay valid wp jwt key rotate --algorithm=RS256 --show # switch to RS256 and print the key pair wp jwt key rotate --immediate --yes # leaked key: reject every issued token now

wp jwt api-key create <owner> --name=<name> --permissions=<list> [--expires-at=<date>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt api-key list [--page=<n>] [--per-page=<n>] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt api-key revoke <id> Option Command Required Description <owner> create Yes User ID, login, or email of the key owner. The owner's capabilities apply, as in the admin: a user can only grant permissions they have --name=<name> create Yes A label for the key, for example CI deploy --permissions=<list> create Yes Comma separated: read, create, update, delete --expires-at=<date> create No Expiration date, Y-m-d H:i:s in UTC. Default: no expiration --format=<format> create No text (default) or json --page=<n> list No Page number. Default: 1 --per-page=<n> list No Keys per page. Default: 100 --fields=<fields> list No Default: id,user_id,name,key_prefix,permissions,expires_at,last_used_at,revoked_at --format=<format> list No table (default), csv, json, yaml or count <id> revoke Yes The key ID from list. A revoked key stays in the list with its revoked_at date The key value is printed only once, at creation. list shows the prefix only. See API Keys for how the keys are used. wp jwt api-key create admin --name="CI deploy" --permissions=read --format=json wp jwt api-key create 42 --name="Mobile app" --permissions=read,create,update --expires-at="2027-01-31 23:59:59" wp jwt api-key list --fields=id,name,key_prefix,revoked_at wp jwt api-key revoke 3

wp jwt auth-code list [--show] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt auth-code add [<code>] [--role=<role>] [--expires=<date>] wp jwt auth-code remove <index> [--yes] Option Command Required Description --show list No Print the codes. Without it, they are masked --fields=<fields> list No Default: index,code,role,expiration_date --format=<format> list No table (default), csv, json, yaml or count <code> add No The code. If omitted, a random code is generated and printed once --role=<role> add No Role assigned to users who register with this code. Default: the Register setting --expires=<date> add No Expiration date, for example 2027-01-31 23:59:59. Default: no expiration <index> remove Yes The code's index from list --yes remove No Skip the confirmation prompt See Auth Codes for where the codes are checked. wp jwt auth-code add --role=subscriber # random code, printed once wp jwt auth-code add MY_CODE --expires="2027-01-31 23:59:59" wp jwt auth-code list --show wp jwt auth-code remove 0 --yes
Setting keys use dot notation, with the section first: general.jwt_algorithm, authorization.ttl, cors.enabled. wp jwt config list prints every key.

Prints one setting. Array values are printed as JSON. wp jwt config get <key> [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <key> Yes Setting key in dot notation, for example cors.enabled --format=<format> No text (default) or json (the JSON-encoded value, for example "HS256" or true) wp jwt config get authorization.enabled # 1 wp jwt config get authorization.jwt_payload --format=json # ["iat","exp","id"]

Changes a setting. The resulting settings are validated the same way as a save from the admin page. Nothing is saved when validation fails. wp jwt config set <key> <value> [--type=<type>] [--force] Option Required Description <key> Yes Setting key in dot notation, inside a section (general.jwt_algorithm, not jwt_algorithm) <value> Yes The new value. Booleans accept 1, true, yes and on; anything else is false --type=<type> No auto (default), string, int, bool or json --force No Skip validation and save anyway. Use it only to repair settings that can not be fixed otherwise With --type=auto, the type follows the stored value: a boolean stays a boolean, an integer stays an integer, and an array expects a JSON string. A key without a stored value is saved as a string. wp jwt config set authorization.enabled 1 wp jwt config set general.jwt_algorithm RS256 wp jwt config set authorization.ttl 120 --type=int wp jwt config set general.decryption_key "my-super-secret" wp jwt config set authorization.jwt_payload '["iat","exp","id","email"]' --type=json

wp jwt config list [--format=<format>] Option Required Description --format=<format> No text (default): one key value line per setting, arrays as JSON. json: the full settings object warning list and get print secrets, such as the signing key, in plain text. wp jwt config list # authorization.enabled 1 # general.jwt_algorithm HS256 # ...

Prints all settings as JSON, or writes them to a file, for backups or for import on another site. wp jwt config export [--file=<path>] Option Required Description --file=<path> No Write the JSON to this file instead of STDOUT. The file is created with 0600 permissions warning The export contains secrets such as the signing key. Store the file accordingly. wp jwt config export --file=jwt-config.json wp jwt config export | jq '.general.jwt_algorithm'

Imports settings from a JSON file created by wp jwt config export. By default, the whole settings object is replaced; --merge changes only the keys present in the file. The command prints a diff ([+] added, [~] changed, [-] removed; secret values are masked) and asks for confirmation before saving. wp jwt config import <file> [--merge] [--dry-run] [--yes] [--force] Option Required Description <file> Yes Path to the JSON file --merge No Merge into the current settings instead of replacing them. Lists (for example authorization.jwt_payload) are replaced, not merged --dry-run No Print the diff without saving --yes No Skip the confirmation prompt --force No Skip validation and save anyway A full export from Simple JWT Login 3.x is converted to the 4.x format on import. # Copy the configuration from one site to another wp jwt config export --file=jwt-config.json # source site wp jwt config import jwt-config.json --dry-run # target site: preview wp jwt config import jwt-config.json --yes # target site: apply # Change a few settings from a partial file echo '{"cors":{"enabled":1}}' > cors.json wp jwt config import cors.json --merge --yes The same configuration can be exported and imported from the admin - see Export and Import.

Checks the installation: plugin, WordPress and PHP versions, the REST URLs, each endpoint (enabled, auth code required), the JWT settings, and configuration warnings. Run it first when something does not work. wp jwt doctor [--format=<format>] Option Required Description --format=<format> No text (default: summary, endpoint table and warnings table) or json wp jwt doctor wp jwt doctor --format=json | jq '.warnings'

Scores the configuration from 0 to 100 (grade A-F) and lists the findings, for example a short signing key or a missing auth code. The Dashboard shows the same critical and warning findings. wp jwt security-report [--min-severity=<severity>] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] Option Required Description --min-severity=<severity> No Lowest severity to list: info (default), warning or critical --fields=<fields> No Finding columns in the text table. Default: severity,code,message,settings --format=<format> No text (default) or json (score, grade, counts, findings) wp jwt security-report # Score: 80/100 (grade B) wp jwt security-report --min-severity=warning --format=json wp jwt security-report --fields=severity,message

Explains an error code from an API response ("errorCode": 48) or a settings save: what it means, the HTTP status, and the settings to check. The full list is in Error Codes. wp jwt explain-error <code> [--format=<format>] Option Required Description <code> Yes The error code --format=<format> No text (default) or json wp jwt explain-error 48 # constant ERR_AUTHENTICATION_WRONG_CREDENTIALS # http_status 401 # explanation Wrong username/email or password. ...

Reads the audit log. Audit Logs must be enabled for new entries to be recorded; existing entries can be read when it is off. wp jwt log list [--event-type=<event>] [--status=<success|failure>] [--user-id=<id>] [--page=<n>] [--per-page=<n>] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt log analyze [--hours=<hours>] [--format=<format>] Option Command Description --event-type=<event> list Filter by event, for example auth.login.failed or cli.command.success --status=<status> list success or failure --user-id=<id> list Filter by user ID --page=<n> list Page number. Default: 1 --per-page=<n> list Entries per page, maximum 100. Default: 20 --fields=<fields> list Default: id,created_at,event_type,status,user_id,ip_address,message --format=<format> list table (default), csv, json, yaml or count --hours=<hours> analyze Time window in hours. Default: 24 --format=<format> analyze text (default) or json list returns entries newest first. analyze reports failure rates per event, the top failing IPs, users and API keys, and findings such as brute-force patterns. wp jwt log list --status=failure --per-page=50 wp jwt log list --event-type=auth.login.failed --user-id=42 --format=csv > failed-logins.csv wp jwt log list --event-type=cli.command.success --fields=created_at,user_id,message wp jwt log list --status=failure --format=count wp jwt log analyze --hours=168 # last 7 days

wp jwt webhook list [--event=<event>] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] wp jwt webhook test <index> [--event=<event>] wp jwt webhook logs [--event=<event>] [--page=<n>] [--per-page=<n>] [--fields=<fields>] [--format=<format>] Option Command Description --event=<event> list Filter by event, for example login --fields=<fields> list Default: index,enabled,method,url,events. Header values are never printed --format=<format> list, logs table (default), csv, json, yaml or count <index> test The webhook index from list --event=<event> test Event sent in the test payload. Default: the webhook's first event --event=<event> logs Filter by event --page=<n> logs Page number. Default: 1 --per-page=<n> logs Entries per page. Default: 20 --fields=<fields> logs Default: id,created_at,event,method,url,status_code test sends a test payload to the webhook immediately, even when the webhook or webhooks in general are disabled, and prints the response. It fails on a non-2xx response. The call is logged when Webhook logs are enabled. logs lists recorded calls, newest first, and requires Webhook logs. See Webhooks. wp jwt webhook list --event=login wp jwt webhook test 0 wp jwt webhook test 0 --event=register wp jwt webhook logs --event=login --per-page=50

Runs the daily cleanup immediately instead of waiting for WP-Cron. It deletes expired refresh tokens and revoked tokens, log entries older than their retention period, and signing keys kept by wp jwt key rotate once their tokens have expired. It takes no options. wp jwt cleanup

Update Simple JWT Login to 4.3.0 or later. Deactivate and delete the Simple JWT Login CLI plugin (find its slug with wp plugin list). If General > CLI is off, turn it on. Check wp jwt --help. Then review scripts written for the add-on: Change Add-on Built-in (4.3.0+) wp jwt validate exit code Always 0; scripts parsed the valid field 1 when the token is not valid wp jwt login --password Required Optional; read from a hidden prompt or STDIN wp jwt config set / import Saved without validation Validated like an admin save; --force skips it Setting keys 3.x names Section-prefixed 4.x names (see below) A 3.x key fails with an error that names the new key: 3.x 4.x allow_authentication authorization.enabled jwt_auth_ttl authorization.ttl jwt_payload authorization.jwt_payload jwt_algorithm general.jwt_algorithm decryption_key general.decryption_key jwt_login_by login.login_by jwt_login_by_parameter login.login_by_parameter

Error Cause Fix 'jwt' is not a registered wp command The CLI is disabled, or the old add-on is active Enable General > CLI, or deactivate the add-on Authentication is not enabled. The Authentication section is disabled wp jwt config set authorization.enabled 1 Wrong user credentials. Wrong username, email, or password Check the credentials Please provide --username, --email, or --login No identifier was passed Add --username, --email or --login Please provide --password No password was passed or entered Pass --password, enter it at the prompt, or pipe it on STDIN User not found: <user> No user has this ID, login, or email Check with wp user get <user> This user must complete two-factor authentication. The user has 2FA enabled A JWT can not be created from the command line for this user Could not decode token. ... The token does not have three dot-separated parts Pass the full token valid: no (exit code 1) wp jwt validate rejected the token The message field contains the reason, for example an expired token or a bad signature The signing key is defined in wp-config.php. ... key rotate with the key defined in code Change the constants in wp-config.php You are not allowed to Authenticate from this IP refresh with Allowed IPs set A CLI request has no client IP; refresh over HTTP Token has already been revoked. The token was already revoked No action needed User not found. No WordPress user matches the token Make sure the token was issued for an existing user Unable to find user <claim> property in JWT. An array setting was set without JSON Pass --type=json with a JSON array or object Invalid JSON value: ... / Invalid JSON in <file>: ... Log in again.', true, ); try { return await get(); } catch (error) { if (!(error instanceof WordPressError) || !error.expired) throw error; if (!(await this.refresh())) throw this.expired(); return get().catch(() => Promise.reject(this.expired())); } } // Refresh tokens work once, so parallel calls must share one refresh request. private refresh(): Promise<boolean> { this.refreshing ??= (async () => { const refreshToken = this.readSession()?.refreshToken; if (!refreshToken) return false; const url = `${WORDPRESS_URL}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh`; try { const body = await this.send( this.http.post<TokenResponse>(url, { refresh_token: refreshToken }), 'Refresh failed.', true, ); if (!body.data?.jwt) return false; this.saveSession(body.data); return true; } catch (error) { if (error instanceof WordPressError && error.expired) return false; throw error; } })().finally(() => (this.refreshing = null)); return this.refreshing; } private expired(): WordPressError { this.logout(); return new WordPressError('Your session expired. Log in again.', true); } private readSession(): Session | null { try { return JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(SESSION_KEY) ?? 'null'); } catch { return null; } } // refresh_token is only there when refresh tokens are turned on in WordPress. private saveSession(data: { jwt?: string; refresh_token?: string }): void { const session: Session = { jwt: data.jwt ?? '', refreshToken: data.refresh_token }; sessionStorage.setItem(SESSION_KEY, JSON.stringify(session)); } private async send<T>(request: Observable<T>, message: string, expired = false): Promise<T> { try { return await firstValueFrom(request); } catch (error) { if (error instanceof HttpErrorResponse && (error.status === 0 || error.status >= 500)) { throw new WordPressError('WordPress is unavailable.'); } throw new WordPressError(message, expired); } } }

@if (user(); as user) {

@if (error()) {

{{ error() }}

`, }) export class App implements OnInit { private readonly wordpress = inject(WordPressService); protected readonly user = signal(null); protected readonly error = signal(''); protected readonly busy = signal(true); async ngOnInit(): Promise { if (this.wordpress.hasSession()) { await this.run(async () => this.user.set(await this.wordpress.getUser())); } this.busy.set(false); } protected async login(event: SubmitEvent): Promise { event.preventDefault(); const form = new FormData(event.target as HTMLFormElement); this.busy.set(true); await this.run(async () => { const email = String(form.get('email')); const password = String(form.get('password')); await this.wordpress.login(email, password); this.user.set(await this.wordpress.getUser()); }); this.busy.set(false); } protected logout(): void { this.wordpress.logout(); this.user.set(null); } private async run(action: () => Promise): Promise { this.error.set(''); try { await action(); } catch (e) { const error = e instanceof WordPressError ? e : new WordPressError('Something went wrong. Try again.'); this.error.set(error.message); } } }

The app keeps the JWT, and the refresh token when there is one, in sessionStorage, so the session lasts until the tab closes. When WordPress rejects the JWT, the app sends the refresh token to /auth/refresh, saves the new pair, and retries the request once. If that fails too, the user is logged out. If WordPress is down, the session is kept. Refresh tokens work once only, so the app shares one refresh request between parallel calls. Turn on refresh tokens in the plugin to use this - see Refresh token. Without them, the user logs in again when the JWT expires. warning Any script on the page can read sessionStorage. An XSS bug would let an attacker steal the refresh token and keep getting new JWTs. Keep the app free of XSS, or use a server that stores the tokens in HttpOnly cookies - see the Next.js example. If two-factor authentication is on, handle the two-factor step before you store the token.

Keep the cookie code in one place, app/lib/session.js: const COOKIE = { httpOnly: true, secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production', sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', }; export function saveSession(cookieStore, data) { cookieStore.set('wp_jwt', data.jwt, COOKIE); // refresh_token is only there when refresh tokens are turned on in WordPress. if (data.refresh_token) cookieStore.set('wp_refresh', data.refresh_token, COOKIE); } export function clearSession(cookieStore) { cookieStore.delete('wp_jwt'); cookieStore.delete('wp_refresh'); } Create app/api/login/route.js: import { cookies } from 'next/headers'; import { saveSession } from '../../lib/session'; export async function POST(request) { const { email, password } = (await request.json().catch(() => null)) ?? {}; if (typeof email !== 'string' || typeof password !== 'string') { return Response.json( { message: 'Email and password are required.' }, { status: 400 } ); } const url = `${process.env.WORDPRESS_URL}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth`; let response; let result; try { response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }), cache: 'no-store', }); result = await response.json(); } catch (error) { console.error('WordPress login request failed', error); return Response.json( { message: 'WordPress is unavailable.' }, { status: 502 } ); } if (!response.ok || !result?.data?.jwt) { return Response.json({ message: 'Login failed.' }, { status: 401 }); } saveSession(await cookies(), result.data); return Response.json({ success: true }); } The JWT, and the refresh token when refresh tokens are on, go into HttpOnly cookies, so browser scripts can't read them. If two-factor authentication is on, handle the two-factor step before you save the session.

Server components can't set cookies, so the page sends a rejected JWT to a route handler. Create app/api/refresh/route.js: import { cookies } from 'next/headers'; import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'; import { clearSession, saveSession } from '../../lib/session'; // Pages can't set cookies, so the profile page sends expired sessions here to swap the refresh token. export async function GET() { const cookieStore = await cookies(); const refreshToken = cookieStore.get('wp_refresh')?.value; let result; if (refreshToken) { const url = `${process.env.WORDPRESS_URL}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh`; let response; try { response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ refresh_token: refreshToken }), cache: 'no-store', }); } catch (error) { console.error('WordPress refresh request failed', error); } // Keep the session when WordPress is down, so the user isn't logged out. if (!response || response.status >= 500) { return Response.json({ message: 'WordPress is unavailable.' }, { status: 502 }); } result = response.ok ? await response.json().catch(() => null) : null; } if (!result?.data?.jwt) { clearSession(cookieStore); redirect('/login'); } saveSession(cookieStore, result.data); redirect('/profile?refreshed=1'); } It swaps the refresh token for a new pair and sends the user back to /profile. If WordPress is down, it keeps the session. The refreshed=1 flag makes sure the page tries only once. Refresh tokens work once only, and the route saves the new one every time. Turn on refresh tokens in the plugin to use this - see Refresh token. Without them, the user logs in again when the JWT expires.

Create app/api/logout/route.js: import { cookies } from 'next/headers'; import { clearSession } from '../../lib/session'; export async function POST() { clearSession(await cookies()); return Response.json({ success: true }); } This removes the cookies only. To invalidate the token too, call the revoke endpoint.

This example walks through a complete PHP integration with Simple JWT Login: registering a new WordPress user, obtaining a JWT for that user, and using the token to create a WordPress post via the REST API. It covers the three most common steps in a headless WordPress workflow: Register - create a new user account Authenticate - exchange credentials for a JWT Use the JWT - call a protected endpoint For this example, create a helper function that makes the actual call: <?php /** * @param $method string Can be one of the following: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE * @param $endpoint string Endpoint where we will do the call * @param $data array Parameters that needs to be sent to the endpoint * @param $headers array Request headers * @return string * @throws \Exception * */ function call($method, $endpoint, $data = array(), $headers = array()) { // Initialize cURL session $ch = curl_init(); // Set the cURL options curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_URL, $endpoint); curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER, true); curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST, strtoupper($method)); curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS, json_encode($data)); curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER, $headers); // Execute cURL session and get the result $result = curl_exec($ch); // Check for cURL errors if (curl_errno($ch)) { throw new \Exception(curl_error($ch)); } // Close cURL session curl_close($ch); return $result; }

"@localhost.com", "password" => "my secret password", "first_name" => "my firstname", "last_name" => "my last name", ); try{ // Step 1: Register User $result = call("POST", $domain . "?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/users", $data, $headers); $responseJSON = json_decode($result, true); if ($responseJSON === false) { throw new \Exception("Response is not a JSON:", $result); } // In case of error, success will be false if (!$responseJSON['success']) { throw new \Exception($responseJSON['data']['message']); } $userID = $responseJSON['id']; echo "Your new user ID is: " . $userID . PHP_EOL; } catch (\Exception $exception) { // Unable to do the call echo "Error while registering the user: ". $exception->getMessage() . PHP_EOL; }

"?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth", $data, $headers); $responseJSON = json_decode($result, true); if ($responseJSON === false) { throw new \Exception("Auth response is not a JSON:", $result); } // In case of error, success will be false if (!isset($responseJSON['success']) || !$responseJSON['success']) { $error = isset($responseJSON['data']['message']) ? $responseJSON['data']['message'] : "Error while getting the JWT"; throw new \Exception($error); } if (!isset($responseJSON['data']['jwt'])) { throw new \Exception("The JWT is missing from API Response."); } // Your new JWT that you can use in other endpoints $jwt = $responseJSON['data']['jwt']; echo "Your new token is: ". $jwt; }catch (\Exception $exception) { echo "Error while trying to get the token: ". $exception->getMessage(). PHP_EOL; }

This example builds a minimal todo app using plain JavaScript and WordPress as the backend. Each todo is stored as a private WordPress post, so they are only visible to the authenticated user. Authentication is handled by Simple JWT Login. ▶ Try it now The app covers four operations: Login - exchange credentials for a JWT List todos - fetch the user's private posts Add a todo - create a new private post Delete a todo - permanently remove a post

Before running this example, make sure the following plugin settings are enabled: Setting Value Allow Authentication Yes All WordPress endpoints check for JWT Yes CORS Enabled The "All WordPress endpoints check for JWT" option (under General Settings) is required so that the WordPress REST API (/wp/v2/posts) accepts the JWT issued by Simple JWT Login. CORS must be enabled so that the browser can make requests to your WordPress domain from a different origin. Configure the allowed origins in the plugin's CORS settings to match the domain where your app is hosted.

Send the user's credentials to the Simple JWT Login auth endpoint. Store the returned JWT so it can be attached to every subsequent request. const DOMAIN = 'https://your-wordpress-site.com'; async function login(email, password) { const response = await fetch(`${DOMAIN}?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }), }); const json = await response.json(); if (!json.success) { throw new Error(json.data?.message ?? 'Login failed'); } return json.data.jwt; }

documents.t: Private posts are only returned when the request is authenticated. Pass the JWT in the Authorization header. async function fetchTodos(jwt) { const response = await fetch( `${DOMAIN}?rest_route=/wp/v2/posts&status=private&per_page=100`, { headers: { Authorization: jwt }, } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error('Failed to fetch todos'); } return response.json(); // Array of post objects }

Create a new private post. The post title holds the todo text; status: "private" keeps it visible only to the owner. async function addTodo(jwt, title) { const response = await fetch(`${DOMAIN}?rest_route=/wp/v2/posts`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: jwt, }, body: JSON.stringify({ title, status: 'private' }), }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error('Failed to create todo'); } return response.json(); // The newly created post }

Delete a post by its ID. Add ?force=true to bypass the WordPress trash and permanently remove it. async function deleteTodo(jwt, postId) { const response = await fetch( `${DOMAIN}?rest_route=/wp/v2/posts/${postId}&force=true`, { method: 'DELETE', headers: { Authorization: jwt }, } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error('Failed to delete todo'); } }

Set the WordPress URL in .env.local: VITE_WORDPRESS_URL=https://example.com Create src/api.js: const WORDPRESS_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_WORDPRESS_URL; const SESSION_KEY = 'wp_session'; async function request(path, options) { let response; try { response = await fetch(`${WORDPRESS_URL}/wp-json${path}`, options); } catch { throw new Error('WordPress is unavailable.'); } const body = await response.json().catch(() => null); if (response.status >= 500) throw new Error('WordPress is unavailable.'); return { ok: response.ok, body }; } function expired() { logout(); return Object.assign(new Error('Your session expired. Log in again.'), { expired: true }); } function readSession() { try { return JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(SESSION_KEY)); } catch { return null; } } function saveSession(data) { // refresh_token is only there when refresh tokens are turned on in WordPress. sessionStorage.setItem(SESSION_KEY, JSON.stringify({ jwt: data.jwt, refreshToken: data.refresh_token })); } export function hasSession() { return Boolean(readSession()?.jwt); } export function logout() { sessionStorage.removeItem(SESSION_KEY); } export async function login(email, password) { const { ok, body } = await request('/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }), }); if (!ok || !body?.data?.jwt) throw new Error('Login failed.'); saveSession(body.data); } let refreshing = null; // Refresh tokens work once, so parallel calls must share one refresh request. function refresh() { refreshing ??= (async () => { const refreshToken = readSession()?.refreshToken; if (!refreshToken) return false; const { ok, body } = await request('/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ refresh_token: refreshToken }), }); if (!ok || !body?.data?.jwt) return false; saveSession(body.data); return true; })().finally(() => { refreshing = null; }); return refreshing; } async function authorized(path) { const send = () => request(path, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${readSession()?.jwt}` } }); let result = await send(); if (!result.ok && (await refresh())) result = await send(); if (!result.ok) throw expired(); return result.body; } export async function getUser() { const user = await authorized('/wp/v2/users/me'); if (typeof user?.name !== 'string') throw expired(); return user; }

The app keeps the JWT, and the refresh token when there is one, in sessionStorage, so the session lasts until the tab closes. When WordPress rejects the JWT, the app sends the refresh token to /auth/refresh, saves the new pair, and retries the request once. If that fails too, the user is logged out. If WordPress is down, the session is kept. Refresh tokens work once only, so the app shares one refresh request between parallel calls. Turn on refresh tokens in the plugin to use this - see Refresh token. Without them, the user logs in again when the JWT expires. warning Any script on the page can read sessionStorage. An XSS bug would let an attacker steal the refresh token and keep getting new JWTs. Keep the app free of XSS, or use a server that stores the tokens in HttpOnly cookies - see the Next.js example. If two-factor authentication is on, handle the two-factor step before you store the token.

This example drives a WooCommerce store from the browser using only a JWT in the Authorization header - no consumer key/secret, no cart cookie, no nonce. The whole app is gated behind a login screen: nothing is shown until a token is obtained and validated. ▶ Try it now It covers the full storefront lifecycle: Login - exchange credentials for a JWT (or paste an existing token) Manage products - list / create / delete via the CRUD API Cart - add / remove / view via the Store API Checkout & pay - place an order via the Store API Step Endpoint Login POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth, GET /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate Manage products /wc/v3/products Cart /wc/store/v1/cart, .../cart/add-item, .../cart/remove-item Checkout /wc/store/v1/checkout

Before running this example, make sure the following are configured: Setting Value WooCommerce Installed & active, with a payment method (for example, Cash on Delivery) enabled Simple JWT Login → Allow Authentication Yes (so /auth issues tokens) Integrations → WooCommerce → Enable Yes Integrations → WooCommerce → Store API cart & checkout Yes (lets header-JWT requests skip the Store API nonce) CORS Enabled for your app's origin, allowing the Authorization header and GET/POST/DELETE To manage products the token must belong to an Administrator or Shop Manager. A customer token can still do cart & checkout - it just cannot edit the catalog. See the WooCommerce integration page for details on the toggles and the security implications of skipping the Store API nonce. warning Always serve the API over HTTPS in production - a bearer token must never travel over plain HTTP.

Every request goes through one small wrapper that attaches the bearer token. That is the only "integration" code you need - WooCommerce treats the JWT user as the current user: async function api(path, { method = 'GET', body } = {}) { const base = state.baseUrl.replace(/\/+$/, ''); const url = `${base}/wp-json${path}`; const headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }; if (state.jwt) headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${state.jwt}`; const res = await fetch(url, { method, headers, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined }); const data = await res.json(); if (!res.ok) throw Object.assign(new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`), { data }); return data; } Products - POST /wc/v3/products, GET /wc/v3/products, DELETE /wc/v3/products/{id}?force=true Cart - POST /wc/store/v1/cart/add-item with { id, quantity } Checkout - POST /wc/store/v1/checkout with billing_address + payment_method The Store API cart/checkout writes succeed without a nonce because the request carries the token in the Authorization header and the Store API cart & checkout toggle is on.

The General settings page is the foundation of Simple JWT Login. It controls the API route prefix, how JWTs are signed and verified, where the plugin looks for tokens in incoming requests, and global security options. Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → General to configure these options.

The Simple JWT Login REST API is accessible via two URL formats. Both are equivalent - choose the one that fits your WordPress permalink configuration: Pretty permalinks (recommended): https://{domain}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/{endpoint} Query-string format (works even without pretty permalinks): https://{domain}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/{endpoint}

Parameters can be sent in any of the following ways: JSON request body (recommended for POST/PUT/DELETE requests) Query string (convenient for GET requests and quick testing) Form data (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) The JWT parameter name is case-insensitive - jwt, JWT, and Jwt are all accepted.

Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → General. Set a JWT secret key and choose a signing algorithm in the JWT Verification Rules ELSE row (the required default rule). See JWT Verification Rules below. Click Save Changes. caution Use a long, random string for the JWT secret key. This key is equivalent to a master password - anyone who knows it can forge valid tokens.

The Route Namespace is the URL prefix for all Simple JWT Login REST endpoints. The default is simple-jwt-login/v1/. Change this only if you need to avoid a conflict with another plugin. The value is trimmed of leading and trailing slashes automatically. https://example.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ route namespace caution If you change the route namespace after you have already issued JWTs, any existing links that embed the old endpoint URL (for example, autologin links in emails) stop working.

JWT Verification Rules let you use different signing algorithms and keys for different tokens - chosen dynamically based on a claim inside the token itself. This is useful when: You accept JWTs from multiple identity providers (Auth0, Google, your own service) Different clients were issued tokens under different algorithms You want to migrate keys without forcing all users to re-authenticate at once The rules are evaluated in order. The first rule whose condition matches is used; if none matches, the ELSE (default) rule is used.

Each rule has three parts: IF - a condition that inspects a claim in the incoming JWT Field Options Description JWT Part Payload claim / Header claim Which part of the JWT to inspect Claim Key text The key to look up (for example, iss, alg, x-provider) Operator equals / contains Comparison to apply Expected Value text The value the claim must match THEN USE - the algorithm and key to apply when the condition matches Field Description Algorithm HS256, HS384, HS512, RS256, RS384, RS512 Secret Key (HS*) Symmetric secret; optionally Base64-encoded Public / Private Key (RS*) PEM-encoded RSA key pair IDENTIFY - how to look up the WordPress user from the token payload Field Options Identify user by Email address / WordPress User ID / WordPress Username JWT payload key The payload field that holds the identifier (for example, email, sub, user.id) Use dot notation for nested values - for example, user.id to read { "user": { "id": 42 } }. Since version 4.2.0, the matched rule's IDENTIFY settings are used on every endpoint that reads the JWT - validate, refresh, revoke, autologin, reset password, delete user, the API middleware, and Protect Endpoints. An external token with "id": 1 is never read as WordPress user 1 just because the site's own login uses user IDs. Expected audience (aud) - available since version 4.2.0. Optional, but recommended (for example, your app's client ID). When set, only JWTs whose aud claim contains this value match the rule's key. Otherwise they're rejected with error code 130.

The ELSE row is always present and cannot be removed. It is used when no IF rule matches, or when no IF rules have been added. The ELSE row has four steps: Step 1 - Key source: Option Description Plugin Settings (recommended) The secret is entered directly in the settings form Code (wp-config.php or custom plugin) Define SIMPLE_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY (and SIMPLE_JWT_PUBLIC_KEY for RS* algorithms) as PHP constants Storing the key in code keeps it out of the database. Example for wp-config.php: define('SIMPLE_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY', 'my-super-secret-key'); define('SIMPLE_JWT_PUBLIC_KEY', '-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----\n...'); Step 2 - Algorithm: select the signing algorithm (HS256, HS384, HS512, RS256, RS384, RS512). Step 3 - Verification Key: enter the secret key (HS*) or public/private key pair (RS*). For HS* algorithms, check "JWT key is Base64 encoded" if your key is Base64-encoded. Step 4 - User Identification: the JWT payload field that identifies the WordPress user. Field Options Identify user by Email address / WordPress User ID / WordPress Username JWT payload key The payload field name that holds the identifier (for example, email, sub, user.id) Use dot notation for nested values, for example, user.id to read { "user": { "id": 42 } }.
Rule Condition Algorithm Key IF iss equals https://auth0.example.com/ RS256 Auth0 public key IF iss equals https://accounts.google.com RS256 Google public key ELSE (fallback) HS256 Your site secret

The plugin must know where to look for the JWT in each incoming request. Enable at least one source. When the JWT is present in multiple locations, the higher-priority source wins. Source Default parameter name Default status Example REQUEST JWT Enabled ?JWT=your.token.here SESSION simple-jwt-login-token Disabled $_SESSION['simple-jwt-login-token'] COOKIE simple-jwt-login-token Disabled $_COOKIE['simple-jwt-login-token'] HEADER Authorization Enabled Authorization: Bearer your.token.here You can rename the parameter for each source. For example, changing the REQUEST name from JWT to token means clients send ?token=... instead of ?JWT=.... note The recommended approach is to keep HEADER enabled and send tokens as Authorization: Bearer <token>. This is the most widely adopted pattern and avoids tokens appearing in access logs.

Since version 4.1.1, to prevent CSRF, a JWT from the HEADER, COOKIE or SESSION source only authenticates requests that come from your site itself or from an origin listed in the CORS Allow origin setting. On a cross-site request - including sibling subdomains and other ports - that JWT is ignored. Request HEADER JWT COOKIE / SESSION JWT From your own site Accepted Accepted From an origin listed in Allow origin Accepted Accepted From another origin, when Allow origin contains * Accepted Ignored From another site, when CORS (or Allow origin) is disabled Ignored Ignored Server-to-server, mobile apps, CLI tools (no Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site headers) Accepted Accepted JWTs sent through the REQUEST source (URL or body, for example autologin links) are not affected.

When enabled, any WordPress REST API request that includes a valid JWT is automatically authenticated as the identified user before WordPress processes the request. This lets you do things like creating posts or accessing user-specific data through the standard WordPress REST API (/wp/v2/*) using a Simple JWT Login token - without any extra plugin. Since version 4.1.0, the middleware decides whether a request is a REST request from the route WordPress resolved, not by searching the URL, so query strings or paths that only contain wp-json don't trigger it. curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/posts" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" \ --form title="Hello World" \ --form content="Post body here" \ --form status="publish"
