documents.t: Available since version 4.3.0, enabled by default. Registers the wp jwt commands in WP-CLI - see WP-CLI Commands. Setting key: cli.enabled. While the deprecated Simple JWT Login CLI add-on is active, the built-in commands are not registered and this card shows a warning. Deactivate and delete the add-on.

When enabled, the plugin uses WordPress's wp_safe_redirect() for all redirects instead of wp_redirect(). This restricts redirect destinations to the same host and a configured allow-list, preventing open redirect vulnerabilities. Enable this option unless you have a specific reason to redirect to external domains.

When enabled, the plugin reads the client IP (since version 4.2.0) from the last X-Forwarded-For entry - the one added by your proxy - and only when it is a valid IP. Since version 4.1.1, it also reads the scheme (http / https) from X-Forwarded-Proto, which is used to recognize requests coming from your own site in the cross-site check. Since version 4.2.0, the Client-IP header is not used: proxies pass it through from the client, so it could bypass IP allowlists. If your proxy sends the client IP only in Client-IP, switch it to X-Forwarded-For. Enable this only when the site runs behind a trusted reverse proxy or load balancer that appends to X-Forwarded-For, and not when the web server already rewrites the client IP (for example, Apache mod_remoteip) - clients can set these headers themselves. When disabled, IP restrictions use the connection address (REMOTE_ADDR), which can't be spoofed.

Simple JWT Login includes built-in Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) support, implemented in compliance with the W3C CORS specification. CORS controls which external origins (domains, ports, protocols) are permitted to call the plugin's REST endpoints from a browser. Without the appropriate CORS headers, browsers block cross-origin requests for security reasons. Configure CORS under Settings → Simple JWT Login → CORS.

Enable CORS if your front-end application lives on a different domain than your WordPress site. Common scenarios: Headless WordPress - front-end on app.example.com, WordPress on api.example.com Single-page applications built with React, Vue, Angular, or similar frameworks Mobile apps that enforce CORS in their HTTP client
Enable or disable CORS header injection on all plugin responses. When disabled, no CORS headers are added.

Enable each header individually and configure its value: Access-Control-Allow-Origin​ Specifies which origins are permitted to access the resource. Value Behaviour * Any origin is allowed. Since version 4.1.0, the plugin echoes the request's Origin back instead of a literal *, so credentialed requests (cookies, Authorization) also work https://app.example.com Only that specific origin is allowed https://app1.com, https://app2.com Multiple specific origins (comma-separated). When the request's Origin matches one of them, that origin is echoed back Default example value: * Required for cross-origin JWT requests Since version 4.1.1, a browser app on another origin can only authenticate with a JWT if its origin is listed here. A * entry trusts the Authorization: Bearer header only, never the cookie or session JWT - list the exact origin if your app relies on cookies. With CORS disabled, or this header turned off, a JWT sent from another site's page is ignored. See Cross-site requests. Since version 4.1.0, CORS headers are also added to REST error responses (for example, the 401/403 errors returned by JWT authentication and Protect Endpoints), so browser clients can read the error body instead of seeing a generic CORS failure. MDN Reference Access-Control-Allow-Methods​ Lists the HTTP methods permitted when accessing the resource in response to a browser preflight (OPTIONS) request. Example value: GET, POST, OPTIONS MDN Reference Access-Control-Allow-Headers​ Lists which HTTP request headers can be used during the actual cross-origin request. Example value: Content-Type, Authorization Include Authorization if you send JWTs via the Authorization: Bearer header. MDN Reference

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://your-frontend-domain.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization A wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is simpler to configure and generally safe for JWT-protected APIs (tokens cannot be forged), but restricting to your specific front-end origin is a good defense-in-depth measure.

The Dashboard is the first page you see when you open Simple JWT Login (Settings → Simple JWT Login → Dashboard). It gives you an at-a-glance status view of every feature in the plugin, organized into four groups. Each card links directly to the corresponding settings page.

The Delete User endpoint removes a WordPress user account via a REST API call authenticated with a valid JWT. The user to delete is identified from the claims inside the JWT. Deletion is disabled by default. Enable it in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Delete User. API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference → caution Enable "Require Authentication Code" unless you have a specific reason not to. Without it, any holder of a valid JWT can delete their account.

Every error response from Simple JWT Login includes a numeric error_code field. Use the table below to look up the meaning of a specific code and how to resolve it. Not sure where to start? See JWT troubleshooting. Error responses follow this format: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Human-readable error message", "error_code": 48 } } Errors raised while authenticating a request to another REST route (for example /wp/v2/posts) use the standard WordPress REST error format instead. The Export-Import add-on lets you copy your Simple JWT Login configuration - including Auth Codes, protection rules, and all general settings - from one WordPress site to another in just a few steps. This is especially useful when setting up staging environments, migrating sites, or replicating a configuration across a network of sites. Download

Simple JWT Login exposes 39 WordPress action and filter hooks that let you extend or customize the plugin's behavior without modifying its source code. Use them to enrich JWT payloads, send notifications, apply business logic, gate requests, or build fully custom flows on top of the plugin. The hooks come in two groups, and each group is switched on in a different place: 19 general hooks (the Quick Reference table) - enable each one in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Hooks. 20 audit hooks (see Audit Hooks) - they fire when audit logging is enabled and the matching event is selected. Enable hooks first All hooks are disabled by default. A hook that isn't enabled never fires, even if your code calls add_action() or add_filter() for it.

Action hooks let you run side-effect code at a specific point in the request lifecycle. They do not return a value.

Fires before a Simple JWT Login REST route is processed. Use it to validate requests, block specific callers, enforce policies (for example, minimum password length), or log activity - for any endpoint. Parameter Type Description $method string HTTP method (GET, POST, …) $endpoint string Endpoint name (auth, users, …) $request array Full request parameters Throw an Exception to abort the request with an error response.
Fires after a user has been successfully authenticated and logged in. Parameter Type Description $user WP_User The authenticated user

Fires before the user is redirected to the URL configured in the Login settings. Use it to implement dynamic redirect logic based on request parameters. Parameter Type Description $url string The configured redirect URL $request array Full request parameters tip Enable "Include request parameters in the redirect URL" in Login settings to forward custom query parameters (for example, &page=dashboard) that your hook can read.

Fires after a new user has been created via the register endpoint. Parameter Type Description $user WP_User The newly created user $plain_text_password string The user's plain-text password (available only at creation time)
Fires immediately after a user has been deleted. Parameter Type Description $user WP_User The deleted user
Filter hooks let you inspect and modify data before it is used or returned. Always return the (modified) value.

Fires on the /auth endpoint before the JWT is signed. Use it to add custom claims to the token. Parameter Type Description $payload array The JWT payload (modify and return) $request array Full request parameters Returns: array - the modified payload.

Fires on the /autologin endpoint when No Redirect is selected. Use it to customize the JSON response returned to the client. Parameter Type Description $payload array The response payload (modify and return) $request array Full request parameters Returns: array - the modified response payload.

Fires when POST /user/reset_password is called. Use it to replace the default email template set in Reset Password settings with a fully custom HTML email. Parameter Type Description $template string The current email template $request array Full request parameters Returns: string - the custom email template.

Use them to add, remove, or transform fields in the API response. simple_jwt_login_response_auth_user​ Fires before the POST /auth response is returned. Fires before the JWT payload is generated on any endpoint (not just /auth). Use it to append extra claims to every JWT issued by the plugin, regardless of which endpoint generates the token. Parameter Type Description $payload array The JWT payload (modify and return) $user WP_User The user for whom the token is being generated Returns: array - the modified payload.

These filters work with the Two-Factor Authentication integration. Enable Two-Factor in Settings → Integrations → Third Party → Two-Factor, then enable each filter in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Hooks.

Simple JWT Login supports OAuth 2.0 authentication with four providers - Google, Auth0, Facebook, and GitHub. When configured, users can sign in with their existing provider accounts and receive a WordPress JWT in return. Configure OAuth under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → OAuth.

Controls how the "Continue with" buttons appear on the WordPress login and registration page. Option Description Stacked One full-width button per provider, stacked vertically Side by side All buttons in a single row Icons stacked Icon-only buttons, one per line Icons side by side Icon-only buttons in a single row
Each provider panel shares the same set of options.
Toggle the provider on or off. When disabled, the provider's endpoints return errors.

When enabled, a "Continue with [Provider]" button appears on the WordPress login and registration page. To make the OAuth redirect work, register the Redirect URI shown in the settings panel in the provider's developer console: https://example.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token&provider={provider}

When enabled, a valid provider token can authenticate requests to any WordPress REST endpoint (not just Simple JWT Login routes). The plugin looks up the WordPress user by the email address returned by the provider. note Requires "All WordPress endpoints check for JWT authentication" to also be enabled in General settings.

When enabled, the plugin automatically creates a new WordPress user if no account is found matching the email from the provider. New users receive the default role configured in the Register settings.

Since version 4.2.0, a provider token must be issued for the app configured in the plugin. Tokens obtained by other apps are rejected. If your applications still send such tokens, each provider has an option, off by default, that turns this check off: Provider Option Accepts again Google Allow tokens issued for other Google clients id_tokens whose aud is another Google Client ID, on the token exchange and with Allow usage on all endpoints Auth0 Allow opaque access tokens Opaque access_tokens, which can't be bound to the Auth0 Client ID Facebook Allow tokens issued for other Facebook apps access_tokens issued for another Facebook app GitHub Allow tokens issued for other GitHub apps access_tokens issued for another GitHub OAuth app, and personal access tokens Backward compatible, but not secure With one of these options on, applications built for versions before 4.2.0 keep working without changes, but the security fix is undone for that provider: any app on that provider, including one you don't own, can log its users into the matching WordPress accounts. The admin screen, the Dashboard and the AI security-report ability show a warning while an option is on. Turn it on only while you migrate your apps to the configured app, then turn it off.

The full browser-based OAuth flow for any provider: User clicks "Continue with [Provider]" on your login page. The button points to the plugin's login start, GET /simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token?provider=<provider>. The plugin stores a random state in a short-lived (10-minute) HttpOnly cookie and redirects the user to the provider's authorization page with that state. After authorization, the provider redirects back to your site's callback URI (/simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token?provider=...&code=...&state=...). Simple JWT Login checks that state matches the cookie in the same browser, exchanges the code for a provider token, then verifies the user's email. If a matching WordPress user exists (or Create user if not exists is on), a WordPress JWT is issued. The user is logged in to WordPress. For headless setups (no browser redirect), skip steps 1-3 and call the token exchange endpoint directly with the provider token your client already obtained. Custom login buttons Since version 4.2.0, the state check protects against login CSRF: a forged callback link can't log a visitor into someone else's account. Because of it, custom buttons or links that send visitors straight to the provider with the plugin's callback as redirect_uri no longer work - the callback is rejected (error code 129 in the audit log) and the visitor lands on the login page with an error. Link to GET /simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token?provider=<provider> instead, and the plugin redirects to the provider for you.

This endpoint exchanges the code returned from Auth0's OAuth flow for Auth0 tokens (access_token, id_token). Use this when your OAuth flow happens in a separate app and you need to obtain the Auth0 tokens server-side. Enable Exchange Auth0 OAuth code for Auth0 tokens in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → OAuth → Auth0. note The redirect_uri used here must exactly match the one registered in your Auth0 application and saved in the plugin settings.

Method: POST Endpoint: /simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token Parameter Type Description provider required string Set to auth0 code required string The authorization code received from Auth0 redirect_uri optional string Override the redirect URI saved in settings for this request

curl -X POST "https://your-site.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"provider":"auth0","code":"YOUR_AUTH0_AUTH_CODE","redirect_uri":"https://your-site.com/callback"}'
{ "success": true, "data": { "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...", "id_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...", "expires_in": 86400, "token_type": "Bearer" } }
{ "success": false, "data": { "message": "The code you provided is invalid.", "error_code": 72 } }

This endpoint accepts an Auth0 access_token and returns a WordPress JWT. Use this as the final step of the Auth0 OAuth flow to authenticate the user in WordPress. Enable Exchange Auth0 access_token for a WordPress JWT in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → OAuth → Auth0. note Since version 4.2.0, the access_token must be a JWT issued for the Auth0 Client ID configured in the plugin (its azp or aud claim), so Auth0 tokens are rejected when the Client ID isn't set. Opaque access tokens (Auth0 issues them when no API audience is requested) are rejected with error code 79. Allow opaque access tokens Turn on Allow opaque access tokens (off by default) to keep applications built for versions before 4.2.0 backward compatible: opaque access tokens are accepted again. But opaque tokens can't be bound to your Client ID, so any application in your Auth0 tenant, including a third-party or compromised one, can send a token of its users and get a WordPress JWT for the matching account. Prefer requesting an API audience so Auth0 issues JWT access tokens. See Backward compatibility.
Method: POST Endpoint: /simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token Parameter Type Description provider required string Set to auth0 access_token required string The access_token from your Auth0 OAuth flow
curl -X POST "https://your-site.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/oauth/token" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"provider":"auth0","access_token":"YOUR_AUTH0_ACCESS_TOKEN"}'
{ "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." } }
{ "success": false, "data": { "message": "The code or jwt parameter is missing from request.", "error_code": 71 } }

This endpoint accepts a Google id_token and returns a WordPress JWT. Use this as the final step of the Google OAuth flow to authenticate the user in WordPress. Enable Exchange Google id_token for a WordPress JWT in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → OAuth → Google. note Since version 4.2.0, the id_token must be issued for the Google Client ID configured in the plugin (its aud claim), on this endpoint and with Allow usage on all endpoints. But then any Google OAuth client, including one created by an attacker, can get a valid id_token for a Google Account and exchange it for a WordPress JWT of the matching user. Turn it on only while you migrate your apps to the configured Client ID. See Backward compatibility.

Simple JWT Login integrates with five third-party WordPress plugins and APIs - WPGraphQL, Two-Factor, Force Login, WooCommerce, and AI Abilities (MCP). Configure these under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → Third Party Integrations.

Simple JWT Login registers its actions with the WordPress Abilities API, so AI agents can manage and troubleshoot the plugin for you. With the MCP Adapter plugin installed, the abilities are available to any MCP client - Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and others. Ask your AI client to: Explain why a login returns error_code 48, and fix the cause. Check the audit log for brute force or credential stuffing attacks. Review the setup and report security issues. Create an API key for a mobile app. Requirements WordPress 6.9 or newer. On older versions the feature does nothing, and the settings page shows a warning.
Install and activate the MCP Adapter plugin. Skip this step if you only call the abilities through the REST API (see Without MCP).

Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → Third Party Integrations → AI Abilities (MCP) and turn on Enable. The feature is off by default, so nothing is registered until you enable it. The page also shows whether the MCP Adapter is installed and active. AI access​ Option What AI agents can do Read only View settings, API keys, webhooks and logs, analyze the audit log, and run the diagnostics Write only Change settings, revoke API keys, and remove webhooks Read & write Both AI permissions​ These cover the riskiest actions. They are all off by default. Permission Effect Allow viewing secrets Secrets are returned in clear text instead of ********. Audit log output stays masked. Allow changing roles register.new_user_profile (role of new users), register.allowed_user_meta and auth_codes.codes.*.role become writable. AI agents can still never make administrator (or any role with administrator capabilities) the new user role or an auth code role. Allow changing authentication providers The OAuth providers, the JWT rules (trusted issuers), how a JWT is matched to a user (login.login_by, login.login_by_parameter, login.iss_whitelist) and the Two-Factor integration become writable. Allow creating API keys Registers create-api-key. The agent receives a working key. Allow adding webhooks Registers add-webhook. A webhook sends plugin events to any HTTPS URL. Changing roles or authentication providers, creating API keys and adding webhooks also need Write access. The security settings (general.security - safe redirects and trusted proxy IP headers) can never be changed by AI agents. note Turning a permission off takes effect immediately. After turning one on, restart running MCP sessions - abilities are registered when the session starts.

The integration page shows ready-to-copy commands for your site. You can connect in two ways. Option 1 - WP-CLI, locally or over SSH (recommended)​ The client starts WP-CLI on the server, so only someone who can already run commands there can connect. Use key-based SSH login, since the client can't answer a password prompt. # Same machine claude mcp add my-site -- wp mcp-adapter serve --server=mcp-adapter-default-server --user=admin --path=/path/to/wordpress # Remote server over SSH claude mcp add my-site -- ssh user@your-server wp mcp-adapter serve --server=mcp-adapter-default-server --user=admin --path=/path/to/wordpress # WordPress in Docker claude mcp add my-site -- docker exec -i wordpress wp mcp-adapter serve --server=mcp-adapter-default-server --user=admin --allow-root --path=/var/www/html Other clients use the same command. For SSH or Docker, start it through ssh or docker exec -i as shown above. # Codex CLI codex mcp add my-site -- wp mcp-adapter serve --server=mcp-adapter-default-server --user=admin --path=/path/to/wordpress Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json), Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json) and other clients that use mcpServers: { "mcpServers": { "my-site": { "command": "wp", "args": ["mcp-adapter", "serve", "--server=mcp-adapter-default-server", "--user=admin", "--path=/path/to/wordpress"] } } } VS Code / GitHub Copilot (.vscode/mcp.json): { "servers": { "my-site": { "type": "stdio", "command": "wp", "args": ["mcp-adapter", "serve", "--server=mcp-adapter-default-server", "--user=admin", "--path=/path/to/wordpress"] } } } Option 2 - HTTP (no SSH access)​ Use this on shared hosting or anywhere you can't run WP-CLI. Create an Application Password in Users → Profile → Application Passwords for the administrator the AI acts as, then connect to the MCP endpoint with Basic authentication. Only do this over HTTPS. https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server claude mcp add --transport http my-site https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server \ --header "Authorization: Basic $(printf '%s' 'admin:APPLICATION_PASSWORD' | base64 | tr -d '\n')" Other clients use the same endpoint and header. BASE64_CREDENTIALS is the output of printf '%s' 'admin:APPLICATION_PASSWORD' | base64. # Gemini CLI gemini mcp add --transport http --header "Authorization: Basic BASE64_CREDENTIALS" my-site https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server Codex CLI (~/.codex/config.toml): [mcp_servers.my-site] url = "https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server" http_headers = { "Authorization" = "Basic BASE64_CREDENTIALS" } Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json) and other clients that use mcpServers with a url: { "mcpServers": { "my-site": { "url": "https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server", "headers": { "Authorization": "Basic BASE64_CREDENTIALS" } } } } VS Code / GitHub Copilot (.vscode/mcp.json): { "servers": { "my-site": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server", "headers": { "Authorization": "Basic BASE64_CREDENTIALS" } } } } warning These config files hold a working administrator credential. Keep them out of version control. If you get 401 Sorry, you are not allowed to do that with correct credentials, check that Application Passwords are available. WordPress only enables them over HTTPS or when WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE is local. Some hosts also strip the Authorization header before it reaches WordPress. Before connecting a live site Start with Read only access and keep the AI permissions off. Switch to write access only while you need changes. Use a dedicated administrator account for AI agents. Review and confirm write actions in your AI client instead of auto-approving them.

Ability Access Description simple-jwt-login/get-settings Read Returns all settings, or one section, with secrets masked (unless Allow viewing secrets is on), the paths that are read-only right now and the granted AI permissions. simple-jwt-login/diagnose Read Health report: versions, endpoint URLs with their enabled and auth code state, JWT input sources, valid role names, and configuration warnings. simple-jwt-login/security-report Read Security review with a score (0-100), a grade (A-F) and the findings, most severe first. min_severity filters the list. Since version 4.2.0 it also reports authentication with password_hash and the OAuth backward-compatibility options (for example, Allow tokens issued for other Google clients). The Dashboard shows the same critical and warning findings. simple-jwt-login/explain-error Read Explains an error_code from a REST response or a failed settings save (for example, 2005) and returns the related settings. Any logged-in user can run it; only administrators also get the current setting values. simple-jwt-login/inspect-jwt Read Checks a JWT the same way the plugin endpoints do: matching JWT rule, algorithm, signature, expiry, two-factor interim tokens, WordPress user lookup, and revocation. simple-jwt-login/list-api-keys Read Lists API keys. Raw key values are never returned. simple-jwt-login/get-audit-log Read Returns audit log entries, with filters. simple-jwt-login/analyze-audit-log Read Summarizes the last N hours (up to 90 days): counts and failure rates per event, a timeline, the IPs, users and API keys with the most failures, the most common failure messages, and findings such as brute force, credential stuffing, or failure spikes. Also reports events that aren't being recorded. simple-jwt-login/list-webhooks Read Lists webhooks, with header values masked. simple-jwt-login/get-webhook-logs Read Returns recent webhook calls with their HTTP status, with URL query values masked. simple-jwt-login/update-settings Write Changes any non-secret setting in one section, validated like a save from the admin page. Some settings also need an AI permission (see AI permissions). simple-jwt-login/create-api-key Write + Allow creating API keys Creates an API key. The raw key is returned once. simple-jwt-login/revoke-api-key Write Revokes an API key. simple-jwt-login/add-webhook Write + Allow adding webhooks Adds an HTTPS webhook. simple-jwt-login/remove-webhook Write Removes a webhook. The index and URL must both match.

Paste an error into your AI client and ask it to fix the problem, for example: {"success":false,"data":{"message":"Wrong user credentials.","error_code":48}} The agent can: Run simple-jwt-login/diagnose to see the endpoint URLs, what is enabled and the setup warnings. Run simple-jwt-login/explain-error to map the error_code to its cause and the current values of the settings behind it. Run simple-jwt-login/inspect-jwt on a token the client sent, to find out whether the format, signature, expiry, JWT rule, or user lookup fails. Fix the cause with simple-jwt-login/update-settings, which validates the change like a save from the admin page. To find out whether someone is attacking your logins, or why logins started failing, the agent runs simple-jwt-login/analyze-audit-log for the overview and simple-jwt-login/get-audit-log to look at single entries. This needs the Audit Log enabled, with the relevant events selected. To review your setup, the agent runs simple-jwt-login/security-report.

Auth codes and JWT rules mix secret and non-secret fields, so update-settings takes a list of operations instead of a new list. match must equal the item's current non-secret values. Otherwise nothing is saved, so a stale index never changes the wrong item. { "section": "auth_codes", "values": { "codes": [ {"index": 0, "match": {"role": "subscriber"}, "set": {"role": "editor"}}, {"index": 1, "match": {"role": "author"}, "remove": true} ] } } New auth codes and JWT rules always need a secret, so you can only add them from the admin page. Other lists, such as custom claims and protect-endpoint rules, are sent in full. Lists stored side by side, such as rules_url, rules_type and rules_roles, must keep the same length.

documents.t: The MCP Adapter is only needed for MCP clients. The abilities are part of the WordPress Abilities API, so you can also call them through the WordPress REST API, for example with an Application Password. Other plugins can call them with wp_get_ability(). curl -u admin:APPLICATION_PASSWORD \ "https://example.com/wp-json/wp-abilities/v1/abilities/simple-jwt-login/explain-error/run?input[error_code]=48" Run read abilities with GET and write abilities with POST. The same access level, permission checks, and secret masking apply.

Only administrators (manage_options) can run abilities. The exception is explain-error, which any logged-in user can run, without the current setting values. Logged-out visitors can't run any ability. Users who can't run an ability can't list, describe or probe it either - through the REST API or MCP discovery, it answers as if it doesn't exist. AI agents can never write secrets. Secrets are masked unless Allow viewing secrets is on: JWT signing keys, OAuth client secrets, the refresh token key, auth code values, webhook header values, and webhook URL query values. Audit log and webhook log output is always masked, and inspect-jwt only reports whether a signature is valid. The AI access level and AI permissions can only be changed from the admin page. They, and the user's capability, are checked again on every call. Every change goes through the same validation as a save from the admin page. Nothing is saved when it fails. When audit logging is on, changes made by AI agents are recorded as AI Ability Executed and AI Ability Failed events. Audit log entries, webhook responses and JWT payloads come from outside users. An agent should treat them as data, not as instructions.
Keep the JWT endpoints reachable when Force Login restricts your WordPress REST API. Requires the Force Login plugin (or a similar plugin that restricts REST API access to authenticated users only).
documents.s: Force Login and REST API JWT Access

documents.t: The Force Login plugin redirects unauthenticated users away from your site and can lock down the REST API. Enabling this integration exempts all Simple JWT Login endpoints from that restriction. This is necessary because unauthenticated clients need to reach the login, register, and token endpoints to authenticate in the first place - they cannot provide a WordPress session cookie before they have logged in.

Toggle Enable Force Login integration to allow unauthenticated access to Simple JWT Login REST routes even when Force Login is active. caution This integration only bypasses the Force Login restriction for Simple JWT Login's own endpoints. All other WordPress REST endpoints remain subject to the Force Login rules. Since version 4.1.0, the bypass applies only to anonymous requests blocked by Force Login. It never skips WordPress's own checks for logged-in users, so cookie-authenticated requests still need a valid REST nonce (CSRF protection), and errors raised by other plugins are left untouched.
Require two-factor authentication before WordPress issues a JWT. Requires the Two Factor plugin to be installed and activated.

When enabled, users who have 2FA configured in the Two Factor plugin must complete a second authentication step before receiving a full JWT. The flow is: Client sends credentials to POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth. Instead of a full JWT, the response contains a short-lived interim JWT. Client submits the interim JWT and the user's 2FA code to POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/2fa. On success, a full JWT (and optional refresh token) is returned - identical to a normal auth response. Users without 2FA configured receive a full JWT directly from step 1, as usual.

Since version 4.2.0, these rules apply to POST /auth/2fa and to the OAuth two-factor login form: Each wrong code counts as a failed attempt for the Two Factor plugin, so its rate limit applies (error code 108). Requesting a new interim JWT from /auth doesn't reset the counter - only a valid code does. Each wrong code also fires wp_login_failed, so brute-force plugins can block the client. After too many wrong codes (30 by default, set with the Two Factor filter two_factor_failed_attempt_limit), the user's password is reset and the user and the admin are emailed, as on wp-login.php. The call answers error code 109 with a message asking the user to check their email. The user must set a new password before logging in again. An interim JWT can be exchanged for a JWT only once. After a valid code, call POST /auth again to start a new two-factor login.

How long the interim JWT (issued after the password check, before 2FA verification) remains valid. Range: 1-60 minutes. A short TTL (for example, 5 minutes) minimizes the window in which an intercepted interim JWT could be misused.

Method: POST Endpoint: /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/2fa Parameter Type Description JWT required string The interim JWT returned by the /auth endpoint code required string The 2FA code from the user's authenticator app or email Example: curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/2fa" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"JWT":"INTERIM_JWT","code":"123456"}' Response (success): { "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." } } note Users who have 2FA enabled in the Two Factor plugin but need to allow API logins without the 2FA step can use the two_factor_user_api_login_enable WordPress filter. This is a filter provided by the Two Factor plugin itself, not by Simple JWT Login.
Authenticate the WooCommerce REST API and Store API with a JWT. Requires the WooCommerce plugin to be installed and activated.

When a JWT is sent on a WooCommerce REST request, the plugin authenticates the request as the identified WordPress user before WooCommerce checks permissions. This lets you drive the store with a JWT instead of a consumer key / secret. It covers every /wc/ route: Classic CRUD API (/wc/v3, /wc/v2, /wc/v1) - products, orders, customers, coupons, and settings Store API (/wc/store/v1) - the customer-facing cart & checkout used by headless storefronts. This works even when the global "All WordPress endpoints check for JWT" middleware is disabled - it is scoped to WooCommerce routes only. Since version 4.1.0, the plugin checks the resolved REST route, not the raw URL, so a /wc/ string elsewhere in the URL does not trigger it. Since version 4.1.0, the JWT authenticates only the current request. It does not do a full WordPress login: no session is created, no auth cookies are set and wp_login is not fired, so repeated API calls don't pile up sessions. Capabilities still apply A JWT only establishes who the user is. To manage products/orders the token must belong to an Administrator or Shop Manager. A customer token can browse, manage its own cart, and check out - but not edit the catalog or other people's orders.

Toggle Enable on the WooCommerce card under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Integrations → Third Party Integrations. Send the token in the Authorization header (no consumer key/secret needed): # List products as an admin/shop-manager curl "https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" # Create a product curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name":"Demo product","type":"simple","regular_price":"12.99"}'

The Store API (/wc/store/v1/cart, /wc/store/v1/checkout) normally requires a CSRF nonce on every write (add to cart, checkout). A headless, token-only client has no nonce, so those writes are rejected with: Missing the Nonce header. This endpoint requires a valid nonce. Enable Store API cart & checkout (second toggle on the WooCommerce card) to let requests that carry a Bearer JWT in the Authorization header skip the nonce check. # Add an item to the cart - JWT only, no nonce curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/wc/store/v1/cart/add-item" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"id":123,"quantity":1}' # Place the order curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/wc/store/v1/checkout" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "billing_address":{"first_name":"Jane","last_name":"Doe","address_1":"123 Main St","city":"Springfield","state":"CA","postcode":"12345","country":"US","email":"jane@example.com","phone":"5551234567"}, "payment_method":"cod" }' Security note The nonce is WooCommerce's CSRF protection. It is only skipped for tokens sent in the Authorization header - browsers do not attach that header automatically across origins, so those requests are not exposed to CSRF. Tokens sent via cookie or URL always keep the nonce. Leave this toggle off unless you run a headless / decoupled storefront, and always serve the API over HTTPS. For logged-in (JWT) users the cart persists by user ID, so no cart cookie is needed between requests.

Requirement Why WooCommerce active Provides the /wc/ REST routes WooCommerce integration Enabled Authenticates the JWT on /wc/ routes Store API cart & checkout toggle Lets header-JWT requests skip the Store API nonce (cart/checkout) Admin / Shop Manager token Required only to manage products & orders A payment method (for example, Cash on Delivery) Required for checkout to complete HTTPS A bearer token must never travel over plain HTTP CORS enabled For cross-origin browser clients See a complete browser implementation in the Headless WooCommerce store (Vanilla JS) code example.
Add JWT authentication to WPGraphQL, so headless WordPress clients can run authenticated queries and mutations. Requires the WPGraphQL plugin to be installed and activated.

When a JWT is included with a WPGraphQL query, the plugin authenticates the request as the identified WordPress user before executing the query. This lets your GraphQL queries access user-specific data and perform mutations that require authentication - using the same JWT you already have from Simple JWT Login. Authenticate GraphQL requests with the same JWTs used for REST API calls Protect sensitive queries and mutations so only logged-in users can execute them Works with any front-end framework (React, Vue, Next.js, etc.) or mobile client that supports HTTP headers

Toggle Enable WPGraphQL authentication to activate the integration. No additional configuration is needed beyond providing a JWT with your GraphQL requests. Without a JWT - the request is rejected: With a valid JWT in the Authorization header: curl -X POST "https://example.com/graphql" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query":"{ viewer { name email } }"}'

The Protect Endpoints feature lets you require a valid JWT for any WordPress REST API route. Use it to lock down sensitive data, such as user profiles, private posts, or custom post types, so only authenticated callers can access it, optionally restricted to specific WordPress roles. When a protected endpoint is called without a valid JWT, the plugin returns a 401 error immediately, before WordPress processes the request: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "You are not authorized to access this endpoint.", "error_code": 75 } } If a valid JWT is provided but the user doesn't have one of the roles required by a JWT + Roles rule, the plugin returns a 403 error instead: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "You do not have the required role to access this endpoint.", "error_code": 114 } }
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Protect Endpoints.
Enable or disable the endpoint protection feature. When disabled, no JWT check is applied to any REST route.

Define per-endpoint rules. Click + Add Endpoint to add a rule. Rules are evaluated top to bottom - the first matching rule wins. Since version 4.2.0, rules match the route and HTTP method WordPress actually dispatches. Alternate URLs such as /index.php/wp-json/... and method overrides (?_method= or X-HTTP-Method-Override) can't be used to get around a rule. Since version 4.2.0, requests to the WordPress batch endpoint (/batch/v1) and _embed sub-requests are checked too: each sub-request is matched against the rules with its own route and method. Each rule has the following fields: Field Options Description HTTP Method ALL, GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Which request methods the rule applies to. Match type Starts with, Exact match Whether the path must start with the value or match it exactly. Endpoint text input The REST API path to match (for example, /wp/v2/users). Type Public, JWT required, JWT + Roles Public - always accessible, even with protection enabled by default. JWT required - a valid JWT is required, for any authenticated user. JWT + Roles - a valid JWT is required and the user must have at least one of the specified WordPress roles. Roles comma-separated list Only shown when Type is JWT + Roles. WordPress roles allowed to access the endpoint (for example, administrator, editor).

Controls what happens to any endpoint that doesn't match any of the preceding rules: Option Behavior Allow access - protect only the endpoints listed above All REST routes are public by default. Only endpoints matching a JWT required or JWT + Roles rule need a JWT. Require a valid JWT - keep only the endpoints listed above public All REST routes require a JWT by default. Only endpoints matching a Public rule stay public.

Example 1​ Assume you add a rule for /wp/v2/users with ALL and Exact Match. The rule applies to these URLs: http://yoursite.com/?rest_route=/wp/v2/users http://yoursite.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users Example 2​ Assume you add a rule for /wp/v2/users with GET and Starts With. The rule applies to these URLs when called with GET only: http://yoursite.com/?rest_route=/wp/v2/users http://yoursite.com/?rest_route=/wp/v2/users/1 http://yoursite.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users http://yoursite.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/1 http://yoursite.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/{any_other_path} Example 3​ Assume you add a rule for /wp/v2 with ALL, Starts With and Type JWT required, and set the Default Action to Allow access - protect only the endpoints listed above. This way, all the endpoints under /wp/v2* are protected and accessible only with a JWT. For example, all these endpoints are protected: /wp/v2/users /wp/v2/posts /wp/v2/comments Example 4​ Assume you add a rule for /wp/v2/users with ALL, Starts With and Type JWT + Roles, with Roles set to administrator, editor. Only users with a valid JWT and the administrator or editor role can access /wp/v2/users and its sub-paths. Any other authenticated or anonymous request receives the "You do not have the required role to access this endpoint." error.

Since version 4.1.0, requests from users already logged in to WordPress (cookie + nonce authentication, as used by the block editor and other plugins) and requests authenticated with an API key don't need a JWT to pass a JWT required rule. JWT + Roles rules still apply to them: the logged-in user, or the API key's owner, must have one of the listed roles. Otherwise the request is rejected the same way as a JWT request with the wrong role.

The JWT can be provided in multiple ways, depending on the options set in the plugin’s General settings: Header Request URI Request Body Session Cookie Since version 4.1.1, header, cookie and session JWTs are ignored on requests from other sites unless their origin is listed in the CORS Allow origin setting. See Cross-site requests.

Sending JWT in header​ curl -X POST "http://localhost/wp-json/wp/v2/users" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" Sending JWT as query parameter​ curl -X POST "http://localhost/wp-json/wp/v2/users?jwt=YOUR_JWT" Sending JWT using rest_route​ curl -X POST "http://localhost/?rest_route=/wp/v2/users&jwt=YOUR_JWT" Sending JWT in request body​ curl -X POST "http://localhost/wp-json/wp/v2/users" \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"JWT":"YOUR_JWT"}'

This page takes you from a fresh install to an authenticated REST API call in five steps. Each step links to the full reference if you need more options. All examples use https://example.com - replace it with your site URL. If your site does not use pretty permalinks, replace /wp-json/ with /?rest_route=/ (see Server).

Install and activate Simple JWT Login from Plugins → Add New in WordPress, or with WP-CLI: wp plugin install simple-jwt-login --activate For more options, see the Installation guide. tip With shell access, steps 2 and 3 can be done from WP-CLI. wp jwt setup generates a signing key and enables authentication; the second command enables the validate endpoint used in step 5. See WP-CLI Commands. wp jwt setup wp jwt config set authorization.validate_token_enabled 1

Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → General and find JWT Verification Rules. The rules are checked top to bottom, and the last row, labeled ELSE, is the default that applies to every JWT no other rule matches. On a fresh install it is the only rule. In the ELSE row: Choose an algorithm - HS256 is the simplest choice. Enter a long, random secret key. Click Save Changes. caution Anyone who knows the secret key can forge valid tokens. For production, consider storing it in wp-config.php instead of the database - see Key source.

Go to Settings → Simple JWT Login → Authentication, turn on Allow JWT Authentication, and save. While you are there, also turn on Allow Validate Token Endpoint - step 5 uses it. info Every endpoint except /revoked-tokens is disabled by default. A disabled endpoint returns a 403 with an error code such as 45 (authentication) or 82 (validate token). The Endpoints overview lists the setting that enables each one.

Send the user's credentials to the /auth endpoint: curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"user@example.com","password":"the-user-password"}' Response: { "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..." } } You can also log in with username or login instead of email. For the full reference, see Authentication.

Send the token in the Authorization header: curl "https://example.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" The validate endpoint returns the user the token belongs to, so it is a quick way to check that everything works. To use the token with the WordPress REST API (such as /wp/v2/posts or /wp/v2/users/me) or with your own endpoints, enable JWT Middleware for all WordPress endpoints under General → Integration Options. WordPress then treats every request with a valid JWT as coming from that user: curl "https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT" The plugin can also read the JWT from a query parameter, the request body, a cookie, or the session - see JWT Input Sources.

Plugin endpoints return errors in this shape. Branch on data.error_code, not on the message text (errors on other REST routes use the WordPress error format, with the code in the same data.error_code field): { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Wrong user credentials.", "error_code": 48 } } Look up any code in Error codes.

Keep users logged in - enable refresh tokens and revoke tokens on logout. Lock down the REST API - require a JWT, or a specific role, for any route with Protect Endpoints. Call from a browser - configure CORS for your front-end origin. Let users sign up - enable Register User. Social login - exchange Google, Auth0, Facebook, or GitHub tokens for a WordPress JWT with OAuth. Server-to-server calls - use API keys instead of user passwords. See every endpoint - Endpoints overview. Full working apps - Code examples.

Refresh a WordPress JWT by exchanging a refresh token for a new one, without requiring the user to re-enter their credentials. This is the standard mechanism for keeping long-running sessions alive. A refresh_token is returned alongside the JWT whenever you call the Authentication endpoint (POST /auth), provided the Refresh Token feature is enabled. API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh&refresh_token={{YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN}} PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description refresh_token required string The refresh token returned by the Authentication endpoint. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled in Refresh Token settings. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key configured under Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). payload optional json Custom JSON object to merge into the new JWT payload. Keys provided here are merged with the standard payload generated from the user record.

{ "refresh_token": "YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN_HERE" } With an Auth Code and custom payload: { "refresh_token": "YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN_HERE", "AUTH_KEY": "MySecretAuthCode", "payload": "{\"custom_claim\": \"value\"}" }

{ "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c", "refresh_token": "f6e7g8h9i0j123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567" } } Token rotation is applied on every successful refresh: the submitted token is invalidated immediately, and the new refresh_token in the response replaces it. Store the new token before discarding the old one.
The refresh_token parameter is missing from the request. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Refresh token is missing.", "error_code": 51 } }
The refresh token was not found or has expired. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Invalid refresh token.", "error_code": 51 } }
The refresh token feature is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Refresh Token endpoint is not enabled.", "error_code": 81 } }
Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }
curl -X POST https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"refresh_token":"YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN"}'

$simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->refreshToken('your refresh token here', 'AUTH CODE');

fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/refresh', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ refresh_token: 'YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN_HERE' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 51 The refresh_token parameter is missing, or the token was not found, has expired or was already used (refresh tokens are single-use since version 4.2.0). 81 The refresh token feature is disabled in plugin settings. 131 Since version 4.2.0: the new refresh token could not be saved in the database (500). The old refresh token is already used up, so the client must log in again.
Configure the refresh token feature under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Refresh Token.

Enable or disable the refresh token endpoint. When disabled, the /auth/refresh route returns a 403 error. When enabled, a refresh_token is also returned alongside the JWT from the Authentication endpoint.

When enabled, the client must include a valid Auth Code in the refresh request. The parameter name used to pass the code is the Auth Code URL Key configured under Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).

How long (in minutes) a refresh token remains valid from the time it was issued. The window is rolling - each successful refresh issues a new token with a fresh TTL, so an active client never expires as long as it refreshes within the window. Default: 20,160 minutes (2 weeks).

A separate secret used to encrypt refresh tokens stored in the database. This key is independent of the JWT signing key. Use a long, random string - the Generate Secure Key button creates a cryptographically secure value. caution Never reuse your JWT signing key as the refresh token secret. If one is compromised, the other remains safe.

The Register User endpoint lets you create new WordPress users programmatically via the REST API. Useful for headless registration forms, mobile app sign-ups, or any external system that needs to provision WordPress accounts without going through the standard WordPress UI. Registration is disabled by default. Enable it in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Register User. API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →
documents.s: Register WordPress Users via REST API

documents.t: METHOD: POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/users URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/users Keep credentials out of the URL Send the new user's email and password in the request body (JSON, as shown below), never in the query string. URLs are written to server logs, proxy logs, browser history, and monitoring tools. PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description email required string The user email address. password required* string The plain-text user password. Not required when Generate a random password is enabled in settings. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). user_login optional string The user's login username. user_nicename optional string The URL-friendly username. user_url optional string The user URL. display_name optional string The user's display name. Default is the username. nickname optional string The user's nickname. Default is the username. first_name optional string The user's first name. last_name optional string The user's last name. description optional string The user's biographical description. rich_editing optional string Whether to enable the rich editor. Accepts 'true' or 'false' as a string. Default 'true'. syntax_highlighting optional string Whether to enable the rich code editor. Accepts 'true' or 'false' as a string. Default 'true'. comment_shortcuts optional string Whether to enable comment moderation keyboard shortcuts. Default 'false'. admin_color optional string Admin color scheme. Default 'fresh'. use_ssl optional boolean Whether the user always accesses the admin over HTTPS. Default false. show_admin_bar_front optional string Whether to show the Admin Bar on the front end. Accepts 'true' or 'false' as a string. Default 'true'. locale optional string User locale. Default empty. user_meta optional string Custom user meta as a JSON string. Only keys listed in Allowed User Meta Keys (in plugin settings) are saved. Example: {"plan":"premium","source":"app"}

Minimal registration: { "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "password": "SomeSuperSecretPassword" } Full registration with optional fields: { "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "password": "SomeSuperSecretPassword", "user_login": "myuser", "first_name": "John", "last_name": "Doe", "user_meta": "{\"plan\":\"premium\",\"referral_source\":\"landing_page\"}" }

{ "success": true, "data": { "id": 1, "login": "myuser", "nicename": "myuser", "email": "myuser@simplejwtlogin.com", "url": "https://simplejwtlogin.com/myuser", "registered": "2021-01-01 23:31:50", "status": "0", "display_name": "myuser", "roles": [ "subscriber" ], "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." } } jwt is only included when Return a JWT in the registration response is enabled in plugin settings.
Required parameters are missing. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "The email address or password is missing.", "error_code": 35 } }
Auth code is invalid or missing when required. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Invalid auth code.", "error_code": 32 } }
Registration is disabled, or the client IP is not on the allow-list. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Register is not allowed.", "error_code": 31 } }
A user with this email already exists. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "User already exists.", "error_code": 38 } }
Email format is invalid or the email domain is not on the allow-list. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "The email address is invalid.", "error_code": 36 } }
wp_insert_user() failed or an unexpected error occurred. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "User could not be created.", "error_code": 52 } }
curl -X POST 'https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/users' \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"myemail@simplejwtlogin.com","password":"test"}'

$simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->registerUser('email@simplejwtlogin.com', 'password', 'AUTH CODE');

fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/users', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'email@simplejwtlogin.com', password: 'my-secret-password', AUTH_KEY: 'my-auth-code' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 31 Registration is not enabled in plugin settings. 32 Invalid Auth Code. 33 Client IP is not on the allowed IP list. 35 Email or password is missing from the request. 36 Email address format is invalid. 37 Email domain is not on the allow-list. 38 A user with this email already exists. 52 User could not be created (wp_insert_user returned an error).
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Register User.
Enable or disable the registration endpoint. When disabled, all POST requests to /users return a 403 error.

When enabled, every registration request must include a valid Auth Code. Without it, anyone can create an account on your site. warning Leaving registration open without an Auth Code is a security risk on public-facing sites.

Default User Role​ The WordPress role assigned to newly registered users (for example, subscriber, contributor, author, editor, administrator, or any custom role). You can also assign a different role per Auth Code - when a user registers using a specific code, they receive the role tied to that code. Configure this in the Auth Codes settings. Generate a random password​ When enabled, a cryptographically secure random password is generated automatically and the password field is no longer required in the request. The password length is configurable (minimum 6, maximum 255 characters, default 12).

Auto-login after registration​ When enabled, the new user is automatically logged in immediately after their account is created, following the redirect flow configured in the Login settings. Requires the Auto-Login feature to also be enabled. Return a JWT in the registration response​ When enabled, the API response includes a signed JWT for the new user. The JWT payload follows the configuration from the Authentication settings. If Authentication is not configured, the payload includes email, id, and username by default. Send WordPress welcome email​ When enabled, WordPress sends its default new-user notification emails (to the new user and to the site admin) after a successful registration via this endpoint.

Allowed IP Addresses​ Comma-separated list of IP addresses allowed to call the registration endpoint. Leave blank to allow all IPs. Supports wildcards in any octet (for example, 85.*.*.*). Allowed Email Domains​ Comma-separated list of email domains accepted during registration (for example, gmail.com, company.org). Leave blank to accept all domains.

Allowed User Meta Keys​ Comma-separated list of user_meta keys that may be set via the user_meta request parameter. Keys not listed here are silently ignored, even if sent in the request. Leave blank to disallow all custom meta. Example: plan, referral_source, subscription_tier note Since version 4.1.0, meta keys that grant privileges or hold sessions - {prefix}capabilities, {prefix}user_level and session_tokens - are never set from a registration request, even if you list them here. Since version 4.2.0, the user_activation_key, user_registered and spam user properties are not accepted from the request either, so a registrant can't plant a password reset key and take over an account.
Register a user from PHP Send a webhook on registration

Simple JWT Login exposes a two-step password reset flow entirely through the REST API. Step 1 requests a reset code and delivers it by email; Step 2 applies the new password using that code. Both steps share the same endpoint URL with different HTTP methods.
documents.s: Reset WordPress Password via REST API

documents.t: Send the user's email address to trigger the reset flow. The plugin generates a one-time code and delivers it according to the configured Reset Flow option. note Since version 4.2.0, an email that doesn't belong to any account gets the same 200 answer as a real one, but nothing is sent. This way the endpoint can't be used to find out which emails have an account. The attempt is still written to the audit log, and webhooks and the response hook only run for real users. If you use the simple_jwt_login_response_send_reset_password filter or reset password webhooks, keep in mind that they run only for real users. If they change the response or add a delay, callers can tell which emails exist. API Reference Explore and test this step using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password&email={{email}}&AUTH_KEY={{AUTH_KEY_VALUE}} PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description email required string The email address for which the password reset is requested. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).
{ "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com" } With optional Auth Code: { "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "AUTH_KEY": "MY_SECRET_AUTH_KEY" }

200​ { "success": true, "message": "Reset password email has been sent." } 400​ Bad request - the email field is missing. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Email is required.", "error_code": 59 } } 401​ Unauthorized - the provided auth code is invalid or missing when required. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Invalid auth code.", "error_code": 58 } } 403​ Forbidden - password reset is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Reset password is not allowed.", "error_code": 56 } } 500​ Internal server error (for example, email sending failure). { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }

SHELL​ curl -X POST https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"test@simplejwtlogin.com"}' PHP​ $simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->resetPassword('email@simplejwtlogin.com', 'AUTH CODE'); JavaScript​ fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'test@simplejwtlogin.com' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 56 Password reset is not enabled in plugin settings. 58 Invalid Auth Code provided. 59 Email address is missing from the request. 65 Invalid flow type configured in plugin settings. 66 The {{CODE}} variable is missing from the custom email template.

Submit the reset code from Step 1 along with the new password. Alternatively, if "Allow Reset password with JWT" is enabled in settings, a valid JWT can be used instead of the code. API Reference Explore and test this step using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: PUT ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password Keep credentials out of the URL Send the reset code and new password in the request body (JSON, as shown below), never in the query string. URLs are written to server logs, proxy logs, browser history, and monitoring tools. PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description email required string The email address of the account being reset. code required string The reset code received by email. Not required when a valid JWT is provided and "Allow Reset password with JWT" is enabled. new_password required string The new password to set for the account. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. JWT optional string Valid JWT identifying the user. When provided and JWT-based reset is enabled, the code parameter is not required.

{ "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "code": "MY_CODE", "new_password": "YOUR_SECRET_PASSWORD" } Using a JWT instead of a reset code: { "email": "test@simplejwtlogin.com", "JWT": "YOUR_JWT_HERE", "new_password": "YOUR_SECRET_PASSWORD" }

200​ { "success": true, "message": "User password has been changed." } 400​ Bad request - email, code, or new_password is missing. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "New password is required.", "error_code": 61 } } 401​ Unauthorized - the JWT is invalid or expired, or was already used for a password reset. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "This JWT cannot be used to change the password.", "error_code": 93 } } 403​ Forbidden - password reset is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Reset password is not allowed.", "error_code": 56 } } 404​ No WordPress user with the provided email address was found. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "User not found.", "error_code": 64 } } 422​ Unprocessable entity - the one-time reset code is invalid or expired. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Invalid reset password code.", "error_code": 62 } } 500​ Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }

SHELL​ curl -X PUT https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"test@simplejwtlogin.com","code":"123","new_password":"test"}' PHP​ $simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->changePassword('email@simplejwtlogin.com', 'new password', 'code', null, 'AUTH CODE'); JavaScript​ fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/user/reset_password', { method: 'PUT', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'test@simplejwtlogin.com', code: '123', new_password: 'test' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 56 Password reset is not enabled in plugin settings. 60 The reset code is missing from the request. 61 The new password is missing from the request. 62 The reset code is invalid or does not match the email address. 63 Email address is missing from the request. 64 No WordPress user found with the provided email address. 93 The provided JWT cannot be used to change the password. JWT decoding errors (1-22) may also appear when a JWT is supplied and cannot be parsed or its signature is invalid.
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Reset Password.
Enable or disable the password reset feature. When disabled, both Step 1 and Step 2 return a 403 error.
When enabled, an additional Auth Code must be included in password reset requests. The parameter name is the Auth Code URL Key from Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).

Choose how the reset code is delivered to the user after a successful Step 1 request: Option Behavior Save code in database only No email is sent. The reset code is saved to the database. Use this when your front-end handles its own email delivery. Send default WordPress reset email Uses the standard WordPress password reset email template. Send custom email Sends a customizable email with your own subject and body. Subject and body are required when this option is selected. When Send custom email is selected, you can compose the subject and body and choose between Plain text or HTML format.

Allow JWT-based password reset (skip reset code)​ When enabled, the code parameter is not required. The plugin identifies the user directly from the JWT payload. The JWT must be valid and not expired. Send WordPress default password changed notification​ When enabled, WordPress sends its default password changed notification email to the site admin after the password is successfully updated. tip To log the user out everywhere after a reset (a stolen JWT or refresh token then stops working), turn on Revoke sessions on password change in the Authentication settings.

When using the Send custom email flow, the body supports the following variables replaced at send time: Variable Description {{CODE}} Required. The reset password code the user must submit in Step 2. {{NAME}} User's full name (first + last) {{USERNAME}} WordPress username (user_login) {{EMAIL}} User's email address {{NICKNAME}} User's nickname {{FIRST_NAME}} User's first name {{LAST_NAME}} User's last name {{SITE}} Website URL {{IP}} IP address of the client that triggered the reset Example body: Welcome {{FIRST_NAME}}, Your reset code for {{SITE}} is {{CODE}}. This request was made from: {{IP}} To use a fully custom template via code, use the simple_jwt_login_reset_password_custom_email_template filter: add_filter('simple_jwt_login_reset_password_custom_email_template', function($template, $request) { return " Hello {{FIRST_NAME}}, Here is your reset password code. Your code: {{CODE}} "; }, 10, 2);

Revoking a WordPress JWT immediately invalidates it - the plugin rejects any later request that uses that token. Call this endpoint when a user logs out or when you need to end a specific session (for example, after a password change or suspicious activity). note A revoked token stays rejected until it expires. The user must authenticate again to obtain a new token. Only an administrator can undo a revocation, by deleting the revoked token entry. API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/revoke URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/revoke&JWT={{YOUR_JWT}} PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description JWT required string Your JWT. Can alternatively be passed as Authorization: Bearer <token>. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).
{ "JWT": "YOUR_JWT_HERE" } With optional Auth Code: { "JWT": "YOUR_JWT_HERE", "AUTH_KEY": "MySecretAuthCode" }
{ "success": true, "data": { "jwt": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c" } }
Bad request - the JWT field is missing from the request body. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "JWT is missing.", "error_code": 42 } }
Unauthorized - JWT is structurally invalid, has a bad signature, or the auth code is wrong. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "JWT signature verification failed.", "error_code": 11 } }
Forbidden - token revocation is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Revoke token is not enabled.", "error_code": 83 } }
Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }
curl -X POST https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/revoke \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"JWT":"YOUR_JWT"}'
$simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->revokeToken('Your JWT here', 'AUTH CODE');

fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/revoke', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ JWT: 'YOUR_JWT_HERE' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 42 JWT is missing from the request. 83 The revoke-token feature is disabled in plugin settings. JWT decoding errors (1-22) may also appear when the supplied token cannot be parsed or its signature is invalid.
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Revoke Token.
Enable or disable the revoke token endpoint. When disabled, all POST requests to /auth/revoke return a 403 error. When enabled, clients can invalidate a JWT for all future requests.

When enabled, an additional Auth Code must be provided alongside the JWT to use the revoke endpoint. The parameter name is the Auth Code URL Key from Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). Configure the codes themselves in the Auth Codes tab.

Administrators can list the revoked tokens and delete entries. Deleting an entry un-revokes the token: if it has not expired yet, it is accepted again. These endpoints require a WordPress user with the manage_options capability (administrator). Authenticate with a WordPress session cookie (plus the X-WP-Nonce header) or with a JWT in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header or the JWT cookie, the same way as the API key management endpoints. Administrators only Other logged-in users get 403 (error_code 115), and a logged-out call gets 401 rest_forbidden from WordPress. These endpoints are used by the Security > Revoked Tokens admin screen and are tagged internal in the API reference.

METHOD: GET ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/revoked-tokens Parameter Type Description page optional integer Page number. Default: 1. per_page optional integer Items per page, from 1 to 100. Default: 20. curl "https://{{yoursite}}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/revoked-tokens?page=1&per_page=20" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-jwt>" { "success": true, "data": { "items": [ { "id": 12, "user_id": 5, "token_hash_masked": "a1b2c3d4...9f0e", "expires_at": "2026-11-12 10:00:00", "revoked_at": "2026-11-11 09:15:00" } ], "total": 1, "page": 1, "per_page": 20 } } The token itself is never returned - only a masked hash.

METHOD: DELETE ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/revoked-tokens/{id} curl -X DELETE "https://{{yoursite}}/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/revoked-tokens/12" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-jwt>" { "success": true, "message": "Revoked token entry deleted. If the token has not expired, it is valid again." }
Code Meaning 115 The caller is not an administrator. 116 The id is invalid or no revoked token entry has that ID. 117 A database error occurred while deleting the entry.

Most WordPress JWT problems come from a missing Authorization header, a disabled endpoint, a wrong signing key, or CORS. Find your symptom below. First read data.error_code in the response, then look it up in Error codes.

The symptom is a "missing JWT" error, or a request treated as anonymous, although you send Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT. Some web servers don't pass this header to PHP. Check that the HEADER source is enabled under JWT Input Sources.

Servers that strip the Authorization header pass other headers through. Rename the HEADER source under JWT Input Sources, for example to X-Token, and send the JWT in that header: curl https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me \ -H "X-Token: Bearer YOUR_JWT" The Bearer prefix is optional, unless Require "Bearer" prefix is on. For browser apps, add X-Token to Allow headers in the CORS settings. If you'd rather keep Authorization, fix the server configuration instead.

With Apache 2.4.13 or later and PHP running as CGI or FastCGI, add this to .htaccess, above the WordPress rules: CGIPassAuth On If your host doesn't allow CGIPassAuth, use: SetEnvIf Authorization "(.*)" HTTP_AUTHORIZATION=$1

nginx passes the header to PHP-FPM by default. If a proxy or a custom configuration drops it, add this to the PHP location block: fastcgi_param HTTP_AUTHORIZATION $http_authorization; When nginx is a reverse proxy in front of another server, add: proxy_set_header Authorization $http_authorization;

WordPress didn't find the route. Check the following: The plugin is active. The HTTP method matches the endpoint list. For example, /auth needs POST. The namespace matches Route Namespace. If /wp-json/ returns an HTML 404 page, use the query-string format instead: /?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth.
Almost every endpoint is disabled by default. Codes such as 45 (authentication) and 82 (validate token) mean you need to turn on the endpoint. The Endpoints overview lists the setting for each one.

Code Cause Fix 2 The token doesn't have three parts Send the complete JWT 11 The signature doesn't match Use the same key and algorithm for signing and verification 12, 13 The token isn't valid yet Synchronize the server clocks 14 The token expired Refresh the JWT or log in again 55 The token was revoked Log in again 110 Two-factor verification isn't complete Complete the two-factor step
Enable JWT Middleware for all WordPress endpoints under Integration Options.

documents.t: The most common cause is CORS. Add your front-end origin to Allow origin, and include Authorization in the allowed headers. Since version 4.1.1, a JWT sent from an origin that isn't listed is ignored. See CORS settings and Cross-site requests.

documents.t: Browsers send an OPTIONS preflight without the JWT before a request that has an Authorization header. A Protect Endpoints rule with the method ALL, or the Protect all default, also covers that preflight and rejects it with error 75. Set the rule to the methods you use, such as GET and POST.
