documents.t: Version 4 adds API keys, audit logs, webhooks, two-factor login, and more OAuth providers, but it also changes some API responses. Most login flows keep working. This guide lists every change that can break a v3 integration and what to update. Version 3.x gets security and WordPress compatibility fixes only until January 31, 2027 - see Security.
documents.s: Upgrade Simple JWT Login from v3 to v4

documents.t: Make sure the site runs WordPress 6.2 or newer. Version 4.2.0 dropped support for older versions. Back up the database. Your settings are migrated automatically when you activate v4, and the old format is removed. Upgrade a staging site first, and run your apps against it.

Error responses use error_code instead of errorCode: { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Wrong user credentials.", "error_code": 48 } } Read data.error_code instead of data.errorCode. The numbers didn't change - see Error codes.

In v3, you refreshed by sending the current JWT to /auth/refresh. In v4, /auth returns a separate refresh_token, and /auth/refresh needs it: { "refresh_token": "a1b2c3d4e5f6..." } Turn on refresh tokens in the plugin settings - otherwise /auth/refresh returns error 81. Store the refresh_token from the login response. Send it to /auth/refresh. Since version 4.2.0, each refresh token works once only, so store the new one from every refresh response. See Refresh token.

The new user is nested under data, the fields lose the user_ prefix, and the message field is gone: v3 v4 id data.id user.user_login data.login user.user_email data.email user.user_nicename data.nicename user.user_url data.url user.user_registered data.registered roles data.roles jwt data.jwt See Register User.
Register users with POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/users. The old /simple-jwt-login/v1/register route no longer exists.

When Protect Endpoints blocks a request without a valid JWT, the status is now 401, not 403. Since version 4.2.0, other client errors that used to return 500 also return their real status, such as 401, 403, 404, 422, or 429. Check error_code, not the HTTP status, to handle specific errors.
Since version 4.2.0, requesting a reset code for an email without an account returns 200 instead of 404, so the endpoint can't be used to find out which emails exist. See Reset Password.
documents.s: Reset Password With an Unknown Email

documents.t: Since version 4.1.1, a browser app on another domain can authenticate with a JWT only when its origin is listed in Allow origin in the CORS settings. A * entry still trusts the Authorization header, but never cookie or session JWTs. Server-to-server calls, mobile apps, and requests from the site itself aren't affected. See Cross-site requests.
If the Two Factor plugin is active and a user has set up 2FA, /auth returns a short-lived interim token instead of a JWT. Send it with the 2FA code to POST /auth/2fa to get the real JWT.

Since version 4.2.0, OAuth tokens must be issued for the app configured in the plugin, and login buttons must link to GET /oauth/token?provider=<provider>. Each provider has an option to keep the old behavior. See OAuth backward compatibility.

With Trust reverse proxy IP headers on, the client IP comes from the last X-Forwarded-For entry only. If your proxy sends the IP only in Client-IP, switch it to X-Forwarded-For. See Trust reverse proxy IP headers.

User Identification moved from the Delete User settings to General, and now applies to every endpoint. Check that it has the value you expect. If your own code reads the simple_jwt_login_settings option directly, update it for the new structure. After upgrading, open each settings tab and check that your values carried over.

Try your login, refresh, and protected requests against the staging site. Look at the Dashboard for security notices about your settings. See what's new in v4 for the new features you can turn on. Stuck? See Troubleshooting.

Validate a WordPress JWT with this REST API endpoint. On success, the response includes the corresponding WordPress user's profile, their roles, and the decoded JWT header and payload. This endpoint is useful for: Server-side token verification before granting access to resources Debugging - inspect what user and claims a token resolves to Client-side session checks - confirm a stored token is still accepted before making other API calls API Reference Explore and test this endpoint using the interactive API reference →

METHOD: GET or POST ENDPOINT: /simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate URL Example: https://{{yoursite}}/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate&JWT={{YOUR_JWT}} PARAMETERS: Parameter Type Description JWT required string Your JWT. Can alternatively be passed as Authorization: Bearer <token>. AUTH_KEY optional string Auth Code value. Required only if "Require Authentication Code" is enabled. The parameter name matches the Auth Code URL Key in Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY).
{ "JWT": "YOUR_JWT_HERE" } With optional Auth Code: { "JWT": "YOUR_JWT_HERE", "AUTH_KEY": "MySecretAuthCode" }

{ "success": true, "data": { "user": { "ID": "1", "user_login": "myuser", "user_nicename": "myuser", "user_email": "myuser@simplejwtlogin.com", "user_url": "https://simplejwtlogin.com/myuser", "user_registered": "2021-01-01 23:31:50", "user_status": "0", "display_name": "myuser" }, "roles": [ "administrator" ], "jwt": [ { "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c", "header": { "typ": "JWT", "alg": "HS256" }, "payload": { "iat": 1516239022, "email": "myuser@simplejwtlogin.com", "id": 1, "site": "https://simplejwtlogin.com", "username": "myuser" } } ] } }
Bad request - the JWT parameter is missing. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "JWT is missing.", "error_code": 53 } }
Unauthorized - JWT is invalid, has a bad signature, is expired, or has been revoked. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "JWT has expired.", "error_code": 14 } }
Forbidden - token validation is disabled in plugin settings. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "Validate token is not enabled.", "error_code": 82 } }
Internal server error. { "success": false, "data": { "message": "An unexpected error occurred.", "error_code": 22 } }
curl -X POST https://simplejwtlogin.com/?rest_route=/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate \ -H "Content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"JWT":"YOUR_JWT"}'
$simpleJwtLogin = new \SimpleJwtLoginClient\SimpleJwtLoginClient( 'https://simplejwtlogin.com', '/simple-jwt-login/v1' ); $result = $simpleJwtLogin->validateToken('your JWT here', 'AUTH CODE');

fetch('https://simplejwtlogin.com/wp-json/simple-jwt-login/v1/auth/validate', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ JWT: 'YOUR_JWT_HERE' }) }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log);

Code Meaning 53 The JWT parameter is missing from the request. 54 No WordPress user found for the claims in the JWT. 55 The JWT has been revoked and can no longer be used. 82 The validate-token feature is disabled in plugin settings. JWT decoding errors (1-22) may also appear when the supplied token cannot be parsed or its signature is invalid.
Configure under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Validate Token.

Enable or disable the validate token endpoint. When disabled, all requests to /auth/validate return a 403 error. When enabled, clients can verify a JWT and retrieve the associated WordPress user details.

When enabled, an additional Auth Code must be provided alongside the JWT to use the validate endpoint. The parameter name is the Auth Code URL Key from Auth Codes settings (default: AUTH_KEY). Configure the codes themselves in the Auth Codes tab.

Webhooks let you push notifications to any external HTTP endpoint when plugin events occur - no polling required. Use them to sync user activity to a CRM, trigger CI pipelines, send Slack alerts, or integrate with any service that accepts HTTP calls. Webhooks are disabled by default. Enable them in Settings → Simple JWT Login → Webhooks → Config.

Toggle the Enable Webhooks switch at the top of the Webhooks page to activate the feature. Each individual webhook also has its own enable/disable toggle, so you can disable specific hooks without deleting them.

Click Add Webhook to create a new entry. Each webhook is configured with the following fields: Endpoint URL​ The full URL that receives the HTTP request when the event fires. https://example.com/webhook HTTP Method​ The HTTP verb to use when calling the endpoint. Supported methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE. Default: POST Trigger Events​ Select one or more events that fire this webhook. Each event corresponds to a specific plugin action: Event Trigger login User successfully auto-logged in via JWT register New WordPress user successfully registered auth User authenticated and received a JWT delete_user WordPress user account deleted via the API reset_password_request Password reset code requested reset_password Password successfully changed Timeout (seconds)​ How long the plugin waits for the endpoint to respond. Since version 4.1.0, the maximum is 30 seconds, and 0 (the default) also means 30 seconds, so a slow or unreachable endpoint can never hang a login or registration request.

Add any number of custom HTTP headers to the webhook request. This is useful for passing authentication tokens or content-type hints to the receiving service. Example: X-Secret-Token : my-shared-secret Content-Type : application/json

By default, the plugin sends a standard JSON payload. To override it, enter a JSON template in the Custom Payload textarea. Use the following template variables - they are replaced at delivery time with real values: Variable Description {{user_id}} WordPress user ID of the user involved in the event {{user_email}} Email address of the user {{event}} The event name that triggered the webhook (for example, login) Example custom payload: { "user_id": "{{user_id}}", "email": "{{user_email}}", "event": "{{event}}", "source": "my-wordpress-site" } Leave the field blank to use the default payload.

Every outgoing webhook request is logged. View the log under Settings → Simple JWT Login → Webhooks → Logs. Each log entry shows: The webhook URL that was called The HTTP method used The event that triggered it The response status code The timestamp tip Webhook logs help you debug delivery failures. If a webhook is not reaching your endpoint, check the log for the HTTP status code returned by your server.

Webhook HTTP calls are dispatched after the API response is sent to the client - they never block or delay the response your app receives. The plugin uses PHP's fastcgi_finish_request() to flush the response to the client first, then process all queued webhooks in the same PHP process. If that function is unavailable (see table below), webhooks are processed synchronously before the response is returned, which adds latency equal to the total time of all outgoing HTTP calls. Server environment Async delivery nginx + PHP-FPM (standard nginx setup) Yes - response flushed before HTTP calls are made Apache + PHP-FPM (mod_proxy_fcgi) Yes - response flushed before HTTP calls are made Apache + mod_php No - webhooks block the response LiteSpeed / OpenLiteSpeed Depends on version - generally no tip If your site runs on Apache with mod_php and you have slow webhook endpoints, consider keeping webhook payloads small and endpoints fast to avoid adding visible latency to your login/register API calls.

Use HTTPS endpoints only - avoid sending event data over plain HTTP. Pass a shared secret in a custom header (for example, X-Webhook-Secret) and verify it on the receiving side to ensure the request originated from your site. Validate the payload on the receiver before acting on it.

Create a Slack Incoming Webhook URL in your Slack workspace. In the plugin, add a new webhook with that URL. Set the method to POST. Enable the register event. Set a custom payload: { "text": "New user registered: {{user_email}}" } Slack displays the message in your chosen channel each time a new user registers.

A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a short, signed piece of text that proves who a user is. In WordPress, an app logs a user in once, gets a JWT back, and sends that JWT with every REST API request instead of a password or a cookie.
documents.s: What Is JWT Authentication in WordPress?

documents.t: WordPress logs users in with a cookie. That works for pages that WordPress itself serves, but not for: Headless sites, where the front end (Next.js, React, Angular) runs on another domain Mobile apps, which don't share the browser's cookies Other servers and scripts that call the WordPress REST API These clients need a credential they can store and send themselves. A JWT is that credential.

The app sends the user's email and password to WordPress once. WordPress checks them and returns a JWT signed with a secret key. The app sends the JWT in the Authorization header of each request. WordPress checks the signature and the expiry, then treats the request as coming from that user. GET /wp-json/wp/v2/users/me Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9... The password is sent only once. After that, the app only needs the token.

A JWT has three parts separated by dots: header.payload.signature. Part Contains Example Header The signing algorithm {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"} Payload Claims about the user and the token {"id": 42, "email": "jane@example.com", "exp": 1767225600} Signature A hash of the header and payload, made with the secret key - The header and payload are only Base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone with the token can read them, so never put passwords or secrets in a JWT. The signature is what makes it safe: changing a single character of the payload breaks it, and only the server with the key can create a valid one.

HS256, HS384, HS512 use one shared secret to sign and verify. They are the simplest choice when only WordPress creates and checks tokens. RS256, RS384, RS512 sign with a private key and verify with a public key. Use them when another service must verify tokens without being able to create them. See JWT Verification Rules for how to set the key and algorithm.

A JWT is valid until it expires, so keep the lifetime short - an hour is a common default. To keep users logged in, the app swaps a longer-lived refresh token for a new JWT. To end a session early, for example on logout, revoke the token.

Method Best for JWT Headless sites, mobile apps, and single-page apps where real users log in Application Passwords Scripts and integrations you control, built into WordPress since 5.6 Cookie and nonce Themes and plugins running on the WordPress site itself For a full comparison, see WordPress JWT plugins compared.

Always use HTTPS - anyone who sees a token can use it until it expires. Send tokens in the Authorization header, not in the URL, where they end up in server logs. In browsers, prefer an HttpOnly cookie set by your server over localStorage, which any script on the page can read. Use a long, random signing key, and keep it out of the database.
